author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the tenants’ unions to counter progressive institutional pressure and steer them toward radical goals.

RF

: 

One of the most striking aspects of the housing protests has been the encampments, particularly in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol. What role did these camps play in the struggle?

GPM:

 Encampments are a very common tactic in Spain—from university encampments for Palestine to the current housing actions.

The recent encampment was crucial because it sustained momentum and provided a long-term vision. A single demonstration after Maricarmen’s eviction would have fizzled out. Of course, encampments bring challenges—you know when to start one, but never when to end it, and coordinating unorganised individuals can be tricky. But it sustained the movement.

This encampment differed significantly from the 2011 

Indignados

 occupation in Puerta del Sol, which was driven by an anti-political sentiment—the belief that being explicitly left-leaning or bringing party banners would alienate the public.

In contrast, this new encampment was structured and managed by militant organisations—primarily the tenants’ unions, alongside our organisation and others from the revolutionary left. Not only were political organisations present, but there was a collective consensus that we 

should

 be there. Today, growing the movement relies on maintaining clear, radical demands rather than moderating them (though as anti-capitalists, we don't always agree with the tenants’ union’s direction or negotiations with the government).

RF

: 

Why do you think that shift away from 2011’s “anti-politics” occurred?

Germán:

 A few factors contributed. First, political organisations like ours have consistently shown up in strikes, social movements, and local struggles, earning respect through active participation over time. Second, the tenants’ unions led the encampment with a framework that respects political organisations and shares space with them. Finally, public perception is different because we aren't a parliamentary party—if we held seats in parliament, people might have viewed our presence very differently.

RF

: 

It seems like people were raising the need for a general strike early on?

GPM:

 Tenants’ unions have been demanding a housing general strike from the major trade unions for two or three years because rising buying and rental prices demand it—prices that have only increased under eight years of progressive governments.

The major trade unions traditionally focus on social peace, class collaboration, and tripartite negotiations with the government and employer associations. They were never going to call a general strike against a progressive government—they refused to do so for eight years. So why agree to it now?

The push toward this general strike essentially has two “souls”:

The first is radical, stemming from widespread disappointment with the progressive government’s housing policies and the strategic leadership of the tenants’ unions.

The second soul belongs to the two major trade unions, who believe they can leverage this strike in two ways. Firstly, they see an electoral advantage. They want to help the progressive government win the upcoming elections by co-opting the movement’s momentum, claiming housing reforms failed only because parliament is controlled by the right. That argument lands because it’s partially true—parliament is right-leaning now. However, six years ago when the progressive coalition took power with a left-leaning majority, it also failed to act. The Socialist Party is an institutional party, and real estate capital—developers, mortgage lenders, and banks—is a pillar of Spanish capitalism that the Socialist Party will not touch.

Secondly, the major unions recognise that a right-wing or far-right coalition is the most likely outcome of the November elections. Expecting attacks on organised labour, they are using the strike to reposition themselves as defenders of working-class rights and rebuild public trust.

Given these competing motivations, it remains uncertain how committed the major unions are to executing the strike. One of the two major federations has historical ties to the communist movement, and its militants are actively organising on the ground, while the other may have called the strike on paper without intending to mobilise.

As anti-capitalists, we believe this strike has real potential. Less than 20 percent of the working class in Spain is unionised, so we may not shut down every factory. But we can disrupt normal commercial life across the country.

Political events can serve reformists and revolutionaries simultaneously. A battle for leadership is taking place inside the strike movement between reformist and revolutionary tendencies, and we intend to win it. While the strike’s core demands are too radical for the progressive government to adopt, strengthening our organisations and the tenants’ unions through this strike represents a win regardless of the election outcome.

Finally, a crucial aspect of this strike is that it has been called jointly by all trade unions across the Spanish state. While the two major unions—CCOO (Workers’ Commissions) and UGT (General Union of Workers)—dominate regions like Madrid, Andalusia, and Castile, independent nationalist unions lead in Catalonia, Galicia, and the Basque Country. Usually, nationalist unions schedule strikes on separate dates. In this case, every single union has called for the strike on the exact same day, which is remarkably rare.

author: Jerome Small
title: Carroll’s royal commission: an attack on effective unionism in Victoria
content:
The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria was announced by Victoria’s Labor Premier Ben Carroll in August: his first act as the incoming premier. 

Carroll’s announcement was a response to a years-long media campaign against the CFMEU, the main construction union. It was also part of a wholesale lurch to the right by an already neoliberal Labor government. And it is a blatant attack on any idea that unions should act to raise wages. 

If proof is needed, just look at the first day of the current bloc of hearings. I attended the first day of the commission back in September and sat through the proceedings yesterday via livestream.  

Literally the main point of yesterday’s hearing was how terrible it was that the CFMEU stopped a major construction job—the Gap Road level crossing removal in Sunbury—for a day and a half in June 2022, and that this resulted in traffic controllers winning an increase in wages from the award rate (at that time $26 per hour) to around $49 per hour. 

The horror. This equates to a full-time wage of $1,862 per week, slightly above Australia’s average full-time wage of $1,835 in 2022. It’s an OK wage, though no king’s ransom. With allowances, shift and casual loading, and the plentiful overtime that construction sites run on, this can add up to a decent wage if you’re prepared to work long hours.

To listen to Chris Young, the counsel assisting the royal commission, a union winning this sort of wage for a blue-collar worker through industrial action in 2026 is a threat to all that is right in the world. So much so that two weeks of the royal commission’s rather expensive time is being devoted to investigating how this could possibly have come about, with the express intention of ensuring it never happens again. 

Young spent yesterday sifting through the circumstances leading up to this supposed affront to decency. The CFMEU had a lot going in its favour. 

Railway crossing removals happen on a tight timetable, planned up to a year in advance. The two companies doing the work—John Holland and CPB—wanted to deliver the job on time in order to secure further work. The labour market was tight in Victoria. The CFMEU had already been successful in securing enterprise agreements with most of the big companies doing this sort of work in Victoria. From the evidence led by counsel assisting, it sounds like the CFMEU judged the moment perfectly—just like any union which is serious about taking action to raise wages should, and historically has. 

Both the CFMEU and the Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) cover workers working on civil construction projects like level crossing removals, and since 2014 the CFMEU has been trying to expand its coverage at the expense of the AWU. The Victorian Labor government at that time was uninterested in helping the AWU maintain coverage over these jobs—like Gap Road—and over traffic control work in particular. 

This was a positive for the workers at Gap Road, and more broadly. The royal commission was told that Zoom Recruitment, one of the AWU-aligned labour hire companies providing traffic control at Gap Road, was operating on a long-expired enterprise agreement that paid only the legal minimum specified in the construction award. 

This is utterly consistent with the business model of the AWU for the past century or more in construction, which is to undercut the wages and condition of the CFMEU and its predecessor unions. And to their credit, for most of that time, the CFMEU and their predecessors generally ignored the AWU’s claims to coverage on “civil” infrastructure work (roads, rail, bridges and tunnels).

The commission heard yesterday that the Labor government’s largely hands-off attitude to this demarcation dispute in 2022, which effectively favoured the CFMEU over the AWU, may have been because of factional alignments within the ruling Labor Party. This is hardly a crime, or even a novel tactic in Australian union politics.  

The AWU has used exactly the same approach, of translating political clout in the Labor Party into industrial coverage (and vice-versa), for its entire existence. The conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Union (SDA) follows the same path. The only difference is that the AWU and the SDA have an appalling record of lifting wages—in fact the SDA did the opposite, helping employers undercut legal minimums, until a path-breaking legal case in the Fair Work Commission a decade ago finally ended this multi-billion-dollar conspiracy to lower the rate of wages. No royal commission was ever called into the SDA, though. 

The cost of the CFMEU’s success in their industrial action at Gap Road was a significant focus in yesterday’s royal commission hearing. On a project with a budget of $110 million, counsel assisting estimated that the union's actions led to an extra $6 million being spent. Nearly $4 million of this was in the higher wages paid to traffic controllers. 

Given that the royal commission is costing about $1 million per week, it’s debatable whether the cost of investigating goings-on at the Gap Road project—two weeks of hearings and (at a guess) maybe the same time assembling evidence—is actually more than the extra wages paid. The Gap Road project was also delivered under budget, at $104 million, despite whatever extra cost was incurred after the CFMEU’s stop-work. Hardly the crime of the century then. 

But of course, the actual concern being aired at the royal commission was that this success in raising the rate of wages would be successful beyond Gap Road. Counsel assisting led evidence that around this time, industry sources estimated that if the CFMEU was successful in their efforts to raise the wages (from the award or near-award AWU rates to the CFMEU rates) of every single traffic controller employed over the entire pipeline of infrastructure projects in the state, the total cost might pass $400 million. It wasn’t clear from yesterday’s evidence what the total value of these projects is. 

Unions should be praised for winning higher wages on major projects. It’s bizarre, and a marker of how right-wing the whole environment is around the “big build” and the CFMEU is, that it’s at all controversial to say this. The storm of media coverage from the 

Age

, and the royal commission that is the result, reeks of class prejudice. How dare blue-collar workers without a trade get a decent living! How dare unions raise wages in a cost-of-living crisis that the media would rather us all accept is intractable! This is the real “problem” at the heart of the media storm and the royal commission.

Geoffrey Watson has admitted as much. Watson is the man who made himself famous by inventing the figure of $15 billion in extra expenses that the CFMEU had allegedly added to Victoria’s $100-billion-plus “big build” infrastructure program. In a recent interview on radio station 3AW, Watson stated of this alleged cost overrun: 

“A lot of it went into the hands of decent, hardworking people, who were getting paid at very accelerated rates. My problem with that was that too was a form of corruption in so far as it’s a misuse of public funds”.

“Conspiracy to raise the rate of wages” used to be a 

criminal offence

, punishable by two years' jail with hard labour. To take action to raise wages from $26 an hour to $49 is apparently a “misuse of public funds”, an equally reprehensible crime in the eyes of some. 

Watson is eminently qualified to know when a decent government-funded wage becomes a “misuse of public funds”. After all, this is the guy who (as the 

Australian

 newspaper 

reported

 in April 2016) “described his work at the Independent Commission Against Corruption, for which he earned up to $4,000 a day, as a ‘poorly paid living hell’”. 

It wasn’t clear from yesterday’s hearings how much money anyone else—for instance, the giant companies John Holland and CPB—was making from Gap Road. The project was effectively delivered on a “cost plus” basis, with the state government paying construction costs plus a “reasonable margin” for corporate overheads and profits. 

The implication of some figures presented yesterday was that this “reasonable margin” might be as high as 30 percent of the project’s total costs, which means the company made somewhat more than a traffic controller who had been lifted off the legal minimums. I’ll keep an eye out for evidence either way, but I won’t hold my breath—corporate profiteering from essential infrastructure construction doesn’t seem to be within the scope of the royal commission’s Gap Road investigation.

Much more of the focus in yesterday’s hearings was on the methods used by CFMEU organisers to stop work at the Gap Road site in June 2022. Rather than simply call a meeting and lead a walk-off, which might have left the union open to substantial fines, it’s alleged that union organisers used the legal cover of health and safety laws to gain access to the site and to log a series of safety breaches. While these issues were rectified, the organisers obstructed work by sitting or standing in particular parts of the site. 

Counsel assisting noted that many of these safety issues were real enough. There were 11-metre-deep holes from the piling rigs, for instance, which didn’t have a mesh cover secured and had no handrails around them. Nevertheless, the real problem, according to counsel assisting, was the CFMEU.

It’s true that rigorous enforcement of health and safety regulations can be used as an industrial tactic. This is far from ideal: it’s a lot less transparent and democratic than the approach that was commonplace when I first started in the construction industry in 1999, which was meeting on site, discussing the issues, and voting whether to stop work. The reason health and safety concerns are often used to achieve an industrial outcome is that industrial action is illegal in Australia in almost any circumstance outside a formal bargaining round, which are usually spaced four years apart. 

Management can sack union delegates, blatantly discriminate, and fail to abide by the enterprise agreement. But if a union dares to do more than file paperwork and pray for the best at Fair Work, and instead actually stops work, it faces the possibility of serious fines. 

Unions in the UK can ballot for a strike at any time in relation to 

any work dispute

. Workers in the viciously anti-union legal regime of the US have a sliver of legal space to hold an “unfair labour practice” strike when an employer wilfully violates a collective contract with the workforce. No such right exists in the legal regime introduced to Australia by Labor in the 1990s and tightened in the decades since. 

Many of the labour movement’s proudest moments—the Green Bans of the Builders Labourers Federation in the 1970s; Zelda D’Aprano chaining herself to the doors of the Industrial Court in 1971 in a protest for equal pay; the 50-day strike of Victorian nurses in 1986 that ultimately led to the world’s first enforceable nurse-patient ratios; the strikes and mass pickets that supported the Maritime Union in 1998—these and countless lesser-known disputes would never have happened if unionists had followed the preferred path of counsel assisting, and slavishly observed the laws of the day. 

One of the most offensive things about the media attacks on the CFMEU in recent years, and the royal commission, is they roll this type of legitimate and important industrial activity together with practices which should be driven out of the union movement—such as corruption and inviting criminal gangs into union structures. Socialists and other decent unionists have to reject both the corrupt and criminal tactics of some in the CFMEU 

and

 the bosses’ efforts to use these as cover to smear legitimate efforts to win wage rises and unionism in general.

Calling out the royal commission for what it is—an anti-worker disgrace—can’t mean uncritical defence of everything the leadership of the CFMEU ever did. In particular, inviting members of criminal gangs into union positions, including union delegates and health and safety reps, is a crime against principled unionism. A criminal gang is an absolutely ruthless capitalist enterprise. It’s a disgrace that such figures, some with zero industry experience, were parachuted into union roles while the Victorian CFMEU was under the leadership of John Setka. 

Writing in 2024

, when the CFMEU was first placed under the dictatorial control of an unelected, government-appointed administrator, I argued that the retreat of democracy within the CFMEU had happened over years, and was in large part the product of a siege mentality. Loyalty tests and secret deals replace organising, open debate, and frequent and open industrial action. 

A siege mentality is not an entirely irrational response when the union is under an ever-tightening legal siege, and when industrial action is criminalised. But in the long term, it’s a dead end at best, or a road to disaster at worst. 

A very different response to a siege is to try to break the siege. This would have to involve systematic organising and industrial action, involving wider forces. It would have to include a program of strikes in the finishing trades, where wages and conditions have been a basket case since the Howard government introduced its vicious anti-union Australian Building and Construction Commission in 2005, and which the current government-appointed administration has clearly done nothing to improve. 

No-one should pretend this is a simple process. Quite the contrary. Construction workers face a difficult task in winning back control of their union. Not the least of these obstacles is the flood of manufactured outrage from Carroll’s royal commission.

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us: 

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like young people are doing a lot of the heavy lifting in confronting the far right, authoritarianism and inequality. This is definitely the case in Australia, where the establishment has spent the entire year cringing and simpering in front of One Nation. It’s taken groups like High School Anti-Capitalists to call demonstrations and try to put up a fight. 

We’re ready to take on Pauline Hanson again on 12 November because we want to see her politics driven to the fringes of society. More than that, because we have a vision of a future that is free of all inequality and oppression. 

Join us - we owe it to ourselves and to the brave students across the world fighting alongside us.

Speaking outside her blockaded school in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a 16-year-old protester captured the hope that students all around the world carry: 

"They spend all day telling us who we are, what we can wear, and what we are allowed to hope for. But out here on the pavement, next to my classmates, they can't define us anymore. We are writing our own history now. If they won't give us a future, we will build one right here."

author: Sagar Sanyal
title: Emergency and autocracy in Modi’s India
content:
The far-right government in India led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been increasingly repressive and anti-democratic over recent months. Commentators are asking if the country is in the grip of an ‘

undeclared Emergency

’, a reference to the 1975-77 period of ‘Emergency rule’ by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in which activists and trade unionists were simply rounded up and jailed. 

The current repression is a response to the student and youth protests that erupted in the capital, New Delhi, in late July. They were sparked by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical movement that began on social media a couple of months earlier. The scale and intensity of the protests surprised the regime, as did the mocking anti-Modi tenor of popular chants. While the protest demand was for the resignation of the education minister over exam leaks, the protesters were motivated by visceral opposition to Modi, who has ruled since 2014. The police lashed out using the sort of 

force

 that they typically use in repressed regions like Kashmir. Police fired pellet guns, used nail-studded batons and sexually assaulted women protesters. 

Despite the repression, tens of thousands mobilised daily for five days—high school and university students, middle-class and working-class youth. Not only in Delhi, but in dozens of cities around the country. Alongside clips of police brutality circulating on social media, there are clips of youth chasing police off the streets with their sheer numbers and bravado. There are clips of cheeky middle-class youth approaching police who are away from the heat of the action to ask mocking questions like “Dear Mr. Officer, are you planning to tear gas protesters today?” The government is tracking down incriminating and embarrassing recordings of those events and asking social media platforms to 

remove them

.

Public opinion has turned strongly against Modi’s repression. Among the Hindi-speaking, middle-class, upper-caste Hindus who have been the most secure vote base of the BJP, parents now saw their own children being beaten—just for demanding a fair opportunity in college exams! Ultimately, the administration conceded the protest demand to sack the education minister, a humiliating 

defeat

 for Modi. It gave the lie to the “unstoppable strongman” image of him so carefully crafted by pro-Modi big media. 

Less than three months after the July protests, a new protest movement gripped the nation. It demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar, who has been highly partisan to Modi and his 

Hindu nationalist

 Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and, according to some parties, rigged state elections in Bihar (May 2025) and West Bengal (April 2026). In West Bengal, the BJP won for the first time due in part to the chief election commissioner disqualifying millions of names from the eligible voters list. Deletions disproportionately targeted Muslims, who are an ideological enemy of Hindu nationalists, and who were also an important vote base of the party the BJP displaced—the Trinamool Congress (TMC). 

Following a late September 

expose,

 which revealed that the chief election commissioner had overruled the protestations of even his fellow election commissioners, the CJP and left student groups took up vote-rigging as a national campaign to channel the energy from the July student movement. Demands for the chief election commissioner to resign have been taken up by all opponents of the BJP. 

When a large protest was called for 

10 October

, the state responded by locking down New Delhi. Around 40,000 paramilitary and police laid siege to a sizeable area around the “designated protest site” of Jantar Mantar in the centre of the city. They blocked roads and shut down local internet mobile services (India is 

among the worst

 states for this). They closed over 40 metro train stations in Delhi and stopped over 200 inter-city trains from reaching Delhi. They threatened activists in their homes on the night before the march, this coming on top of regular arbitrary detention of prominent leaders of the protest movement (from the CJP and the left parties). 

Undeterred

, protestors appeared in their tens of thousands and were again met with batons and tear gas, and thousands were detained.

Sizeable protests have continued sporadically since 10 October, some called by the CJP or student organizations of the left, 

others

 by major opposition parties. The cause has received expressions of 

support

 from the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (United Farmers’ Front), an umbrella organization of farmers’ unions that emerged in 2020 in opposition to 

Modi’s Farm Laws

, as well as from trade union federations.  

Many see the 10 October crackdown in Delhi as a sign that the Modi regime fears being toppled. Speculation is rife that India will have its own version of the “Gen Z” protests that ousted governments in neighbouring Nepal (2025), Bangladesh (2024) and Sri Lanka (2022). BJP politicians denounce the protests as a plot by foreign powers to destabilise Indian society and bring about regime change. 

The Modi administration appears backed into a corner. To sack the election commissioner would be tantamount to accepting that several state elections over the past year have been 

rigged

. 

*****

What explains the rage of students and youth? Among young college graduates, 

unemployment

 is at 40 percent. The shrinking size of the public sector means there are fewer jobs for graduates. Promises of jobs in corporate management or in professional and white-collar careers in a handful of headline-grabbing sectors like IT have turned out to be a pipe dream for most, given the large pool of unemployed graduates. 

College graduates are not outliers in the wider economy. Since 2014, when the Modi government took power, it has marketed India as a fast-growing economy with jobs for all and rising incomes for the masses. Yet growing numbers of youth feel that reality does not match state propaganda. Not just young people. The 

middle class

 of India has seen stagnating incomes during Modi’s rule, while the working class faces a 

crisis of underemployment

 that has built up over a quarter-century of neoliberalism.

As Indian capitalists see it, the economy needs major “restructuring”. Private investment needs a shot in the arm. There are too many inefficient’ labour-intensive small enterprises, which ought to make way for big capital-intensive enterprises. Capital resources must be moved from producing for ordinary Indian households to producing for export or building infrastructure to attract foreign investment - especially in military, strategic and high-tech sectors. Wages must be held down. Yet all these measures will further reduce the number of jobs, reduce wages and take national resources away from the goods and services that ordinary households consume. 

The July and October waves of protest in India are an elemental upsurge that carries the potential to make major social changes. Even more so if the protesters can combine forces with workers, who undertook a wave of wildcat 

strikes

 earlier this year, and with farmers' unions who expect a renewed fight against Modi over recent US-India trade agreements which threaten their livelihoods.

What comes of this latent potential depends on its political leadership. There are both moderate and radical sections of the movement. For now, it appears the momentum of protest has been channelled onto a moderate path. Opposition parties, predominantly moderate, see an opportunity to “ride the tiger” of popular upsurge to dislodge the BJP from power. The largest such party is the Congress party, which anchors the “INDIA bloc” of parties that oppose the BJP and aspire to form a coalition government. This bloc of parties organised the most recent large rally, on November 1 in New Delhi, rather than the CJP or the left student groups associated with the explosive protests in July and early October. 

Besides Congress, several parties with a provincial or sub-national presence are also important. They represent blocs of provincial capital that have distinct interests to the capitalists who dominate national policy. They have sizeable vote bases among castes and communities special to their province. The Samajwadi Party, for instance, is a big presence in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, currently governed by a BJP firebrand but facing elections in the early months of 2027. The TMC was entrenched in West Bengal until its loss to the BJP this year. These parties are keen to reform the election commission to ensure their own survival against the BJP. However, like the BJP, they too want to rule in favour of the capitalist class and are loath to address the deeper economic grievances fuelling the upsurge.

The protest movement has also spurred mainstream discussion of Hindu nationalist forces beyond the Modi administration. The Indian far-right is bigger than Modi and his immediate crew. It is highly organised and ideological. At its centre lies the 

RSS

, a disciplined, cadre-based Hindu supremacist organization created in the 1920s, which explicitly drew on the fascism of Mussolini and Hitler. The RSS does not contest elections but is the controlling force behind the BJP. Modi has been an RSS man since childhood. Around the RSS are various vigilante groups. Under the Modi government, RSS men have been increasingly inserted into the state bureaucracy, judiciary, the police and armed forces, university leaderships, and, of course, the election commission. In BJP-ruled states, Hindu nationalist vigilante groups have developed working relations with police. These groups routinely 

lynch

 and beat Muslims without police interference. 

It would be one thing to remove from the helm of the state Modi and his right-hand man Amit Shah, the Home Minister. But that would leave intact a state machinery peppered with ideologically cohered and well-connected right-wingers. They are practised in suppressing democracy and pushing Hindu supremacy in league with vigilantes. 

In recent weeks, speeches by Congress leader Gandhi have targeted not only Modi and the BJP but also the RSS and its supreme leader Mohan Bhagwat. This plays well for a progressive audience, who have long been alarmed by the growing threat of the RSS. However, if the attacks on the RSS go beyond rhetoric and have the effect of encouraging efforts to clean out the state machinery of notorious RSS personnel, it is possible this will open space for more radical sections of the protesters to revive and take momentum back from the moderates.

It remains to be seen what will be gained out of the youth upsurges of July and early October. Some lessons are already apparent. The explosive power of discontented youth could place on the back foot a Modi regime that has seemed unstoppable. Indian progressives had despaired for years about the steady erosion of democracy and bemoaned the failure of the mainstream opposition parties to resist. Today, there is hope.

author: Rick Kuhn
title: Unemployment: a feature of capitalism, not a bug
content:
Today more than one in ten workers can’t find enough paid labour to live a decent life. And that’s only workers actively looking for a job or for more hours of employment. It doesn’t count those who have given up on finding a job, even though they want one, and survive thanks to friends, family or a measly government payment that isn’t an unemployment benefit.

In September

 the seasonally adjusted 

un

employment rate was 4.7 percent; 

under

employment was 6.3 percent. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, you’re not unemployed if you worked even an hour in the survey fortnight.

To get the Jobseeker Payment or Youth Allowance the un- and underemployed have to follow the Albanese government’s savage eligibility rules, inherited from its Liberal predecessors. If you earn more than a pitiful $75 a week, your payment starts to go down. You must follow the instructions of Workforce Australia and, if you’ve been directed to one, of an outsourced “employment services provider” agency, which profits from government funding.

That may mean applying for a certain number of jobs every “reporting period”, doing training they tell you to do, however meaningless courses about writing job applications or behaviour during an interview might be; or perform “work for the dole”, that would normally be done for much higher award wages. You have to “accept any offer of suitable paid work”, defined by the provider, whether the type of work or its location actually suits you or not.

If you’re single, without kids, the dole is 

currently

 

a princely $413 a week. Certainly in Sydney, you’d be very lucky if less than half of that went on renting a room. And if you’re young, that’s unfortunate: unemployed aged 21 or younger are penalised and get less money than those over 21. Apparently young people don’t need as much shelter, food, clothing, etc. as older people.

Both the unemployment and underemployment rates are rising.

Unemployment is not a bug in capitalism, but a feature. The threat of un- and underemployment – descending into what Marx called “

the industrial reserve army

”—disciplines workers fearful of losing their jobs. The higher the level of unemployment, other things being equal, the less likely they are to take risks by fighting to defend or improve their pay and conditions.

The extent of the reserve army of labour changes in the course of economic cycles: lower during booms, higher in slumps.

Many central banks, like the Reserve Bank of Australia, are bumping up interest rates to slow their countries’ economies down. Their goal is not increased unemployment; that’s a side effect. Their main target is the rate of inflation. High inflation—lack of stability in the purchasing power of money—makes calculations by capitalists about their activities and especially investments more difficult. 

In legislation

, the RBA has two goals: “price stability and the maintenance of full employment”. It says that “

[t]hese two objectives usually work together

”. In practice, the bank favours sacrificing jobs to keep a lid on inflation.

But today, high oil prices, due to the USA’s and Israel’s war on Iran, is the main driver of inflation. The RBA isn’t bumping up interest rates to discipline workers, although that’s a side-effect. Governor 

Michelle Bullock 

said at the end of September that “There is no wage price spiral going on in Australia. Rises in wages are not driving … cost pressures”.

In fact, it is workers who are mainly affected by inflation. Greg Jericho, in the 

Guardian

, has illustrated how workers’ real pay has been falling since 2021, compared with the Consumer Price Index by 7 percent; compared with the more appropriate Employee Living Cost Index, by more than 12 percent.

The hostility of most union officials to leading their members in serious struggles to defend, let alone restore or improve their living standards, is mainly to blame.

In his 1972 report 

Poverty in Australia

, Ronald Henderson, appointed by the Liberal government of Billy McMahon, calculated a poverty line, marking an “austere” standard of living below which people were in poverty. The Melbourne Institute of Economic Research frequently updates it. 

JobSeeker 

has consistently been below this line. Today that unemployment benefit is less than half the 

Henderson poverty line

. Using 50, let alone 60 percent of median 

household income

, common alternative international measures of poverty, the situation of people on JobSeeker is even worse.

Consequently, people on unemployment benefits are much more prone to illness and death. In 2022, the government’s own Australian Institute of Health and Welfare calculated that the death rate of people on unemployment benefits was five times 

higher

 than of those who weren’t on an unemployment, parenting or carer payment, or Disability Support Pension. The mortality rate of the unemployed fell dramatically during the COVID crisis, when Scott Morrison’s Liberal government made temporarily higher payments available, to avoid a revolt prompted by the 

sudden increase

 in unemployment by almost half to 7.5 percent.

In 1993, during the last severe recession in Australia, 

unemployment climbed

 to 10.9 percent. Recurrent economic crises are built into capitalism. Whether the next one is triggered by over-zealous action by the Reserve Bank, the collapse of the AI investment bubble or something else, the number of people living in poverty will skyrocket again, and a repeat of Morrison’s “generosity” to them, by a Labor, Liberal or One Nation government, is exceptionally unlikely.

author: Priya T.
title: Workers can overthrow capitalism
content:
Human beings are the most cooperative species that have ever existed. The expectation that we will live socially, with other people to help and guide us, is built into our biology. 

Compare a human baby with, say, crocodiles, which are born with as many as 60 teeth and use them to break through their eggshell, fending for themselves from their earliest moments. Or baby horses, who can walk within an hour of birth. Human babies can’t so much as lift their own heads

. 

Our evolutionary survival instinct is to 

cry

, the single purpose of which is to 

alert others

 to needs or distress. This interdependence continues, in various ways, throughout our lives.

The fact that humans are not designed to make it alone is why capitalism feels so deeply wrong to so many of us. It is not geared towards meeting people’s needs, and the values it promotes—individualism, competition and greed—run counter to the social and collective instincts that are crucial to our survival as a species. 

The enormous resources and technologies that capitalism brings into existence are not used to provide for people or distributed to meet need. Instead, they are bought and sold to generate wealth for the tiny minority who control them. This gap between how things are, and how they could and should be, is one of the features of the system that perpetually cause people to turn against it. And it is becoming increasingly obscene. 

At the same time as the super-rich are getting on commercial space flights—at $70 million a ticket—the majority of the world’s population have never set foot on a plane. While the ultra-wealthy pour resources into the pursuit of immortality 

for themselves, 

wasting millions on cryogenic chambers, organ replacement, blood transfusions and uploading themselves to the cloud, millions of children die from diarrhea-related illnesses every year, and 3.4 billion people live without proper sanitation. Twelve billionaires hold more wealth than half of humanity. Abundance exists, but it is hoarded away from the masses. 

The rich would like us to think they earned and therefore deserve this wealth; that they are compensated in proportion to what they contribute to society. Australia’s richest person Gina Rinehart wrote a column expressing this view for the industry publication 

Australian Resources and Investment 

in 2012: “If you’re jealous of those with more money, don’t just sit there and complain; do something to make more money yourself—spend less time drinking, or smoking, or socialising, and more time working.” 

Leaving aside that Rinehart seems to spend heaps of time drinking and socialising, including at expensive Italian hotels with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, nobody really thinks that a mining executive works harder than a garbage truck driver or early childhood educator. But the reality is that on average Australian salaries, it would take these workers about 650,000 years of “more time working” to earn the $40 billion Rinehart is worth. 

The truth is that the ruling class amasses their wealth not by working harder than everyone else, but by getting 

other people to work for them

. Wealth is “created” when the value of the products other people produce is greater than what they are paid by their bosses in wages. This is called exploitation, and it is the basis of capital accumulation. 

Without the labour of workers, bosses wouldn’t have profits or power. Workers do the work to produce what we all need, while the “work” bosses do is to protect their control over this process, make it more profitable and manage the profits. This control gives bosses the ability to shape the lives of millions if not billions of other people—they decide what is made, who gets it and what it sells for. 

The majority, on the other hand, are oppressed: they are denied control over their own activity, as well as what happens to the products of their labour and, by extension, how their society is organised. This oppression is a prerequisite for exploitation—workers are conditioned from birth into accepting their subordinate place in society, and are expected to accept it throughout their working lives. Whether this is unadulterated, as in tyrannical dictatorships, or sanitised, as in parliamentary democracies, the underlying reality is the same. Bosses exercise dictatorial authority in the workplace. And their interests inform government policy. 

The majority of us get little to no say over what happens in our communities, despite living there. Nobody asks residents if they want data centres plonked in their neighbourhoods, for example, or a McDonalds on every shopping strip. Unless collective action forces the outcome to be different, politicians and corporations get to do whatever they want because they hold economic and political power. 

Workers can’t just opt out of this system. To survive, most people need to earn a wage, or depend on someone who does. The prospect of a life where you can’t pay for things is so terrible, that for most people, most of the time, it is preferable to make peace with exploitation and the accompanying lack of control. If the alternative is poverty, it can feel preferable to follow the unfair rules bosses lay down; to “suck it up” when life is unsatisfying and “get over it” when the world makes you sick and sad, and shrinks your dreams. 

The fact that nearly half of young people in Australia, according to a 2025 Headspace survey, reported experiencing high or very high psychological distress, speaks to a society that is broken. The future is especially bleak if you’re young. Some life goals previous generations might have taken for granted, like owning a home and having a stable job, are increasingly out of reach. Meanwhile, the future of the planet is in jeopardy and no-one in power cares enough to act, and tech experts are warning that AI, already widely resented, may soon wipe out our species. It is perfectly rational for young people to feel panic or despair watching all this. Rational, too, for this reality to make someone want to barricade their school. Or throw a trash can through a window.

Capitalism has brought the world to extremes of inequality and degraded the majority of people materially and morally. So is there hope? Yes, there is. 

Workers are not merely victims. At the same time as being exploited, oppressed and alienated, workers are cooperative, able to produce everything we need to survive, and potentially extremely powerful. And they don’t have a stake in the status quo. 

Billions of workers around the world are connected to each other through the labour process. Despite the ideology of individualism, workers are mutually dependent on each other, and, at a local and global level, are only able to produce the things we all need collectively. This means the ability to cooperate is built into working class life in a way it is not for bosses. And workers everywhere share not only the labour process, but also the antagonistic relationship with their bosses—bosses everywhere want workers to work harder for less to maximise profit, while workers want the opposite.

In fact, it is 

because 

workers are structurally united in this way that the system requires division and repression. The ruling class have a variety of tools at their disposal to maintain their social position, from the brute force of police and soldiers, to spreading hateful ideologies like racism through the media or politics. They need scapegoats and enforcement mechanisms because fundamentally, the capitalists’ wealth and privilege rests upon workers accepting their exploitation, and not realising the common interest they share with other workers. 

These containment measures can only be so effective, because capitalism repeatedly gives workers reasons to rebel. Workers can be compelled to resist out of frustration with a steady erosion of their rights, by attacks on their wages or conditions, a significant shock to society like a war or economic crisis, or through disgust with the moral depravity of capitalism. And because the system has an integrated purpose—profit making—when workers get angry about one issue, it often leads them to question other aspects of the system too. 

When workers stand together and start to take action, it shatters the optical illusions that make capitalism seem all-powerful. Instead of spending their days checking off tasks set by capitalist managers, in times of struggle workers take collective control over their workplaces, and start consciously directing the labour they already do, using the skills and knowledge they already possess. 

Democracy is essential to these sorts of working-class rebellions. Workers can only exercise their power collectively, which means it is essential that all participants feel invested in the struggle. This means everyone needs a voice and a say, and disagreements have to be debated out until a collective decision can be reached that people are happy to stick to. Dictating to others weakens the unity workers draw their strength from. 

For this reason, and contrary to the stereotypes, revolutions involve a lot more talking and debate than they do violent uprising. This sort of collective organising often centres around places and activities where people ordinarily gather; schools and universities, neighbourhoods, and, crucially, workplaces. 

Importantly at work, talk can translate into action. Workers have the practical, hands on, down-to-earth skills to bridge the gap between how the world is and how it should be. Electricians, forklift operators, delivery drivers and supermarket workers can not only come up with a plan for moving resources around to get food on every table, they could make it happen. Workers could distribute resources for human need and not profit if they performed their labour collectively and consciously. 

To do this on a larger scale, workers also need wider organising and coordinating bodies, which means more talking and discussion. This is crucial to the process of revolution: to succeed, workers must create their own institutions for governing the economy and society, rooted in their collective power and able to coordinate the conscious, democratic organisation of labour. Bodies like these have been repeatedly created in workers’ revolutions throughout history. 

When workers start to organise on this scale, it is an acute challenge to the existing order. The state, with its wide reach and ability to intimidate through organised violence, is mobilised to force workers back into their place. A revolution therefore needs to defend itself from the old order at the same time as it creates a new one, which means dismantling the capitalist state. 

None of this is easy. The capitalist class is very sensitive to any challenge to its power, while workers are not used to exercising theirs. And action has to be taken quickly and decisively when struggles erupt—workers are much more prone to losing their nerve than the capitalist class. Having a large current of organised revolutionaries prior to massive struggles breaking out, with a clear idea of what is needed to overthrow capitalism and establish workers’ power, is an indispensable tool. Such organisation needs to be built before revolutions begin; it is too late to get organised once things start to move. This is why Socialist Alternative argues we need to be organised today, not because revolution is imminent, but because building our forces in the less explosive times is necessary. 

A world run by workers has the potential to replace profit making with rational organisation: to go from a society in service of the wealthy to one that serves us all. No more deprivation alongside excess; no more reducing human beings to cogs in a machine. If the majority had real control over their labour, and real control over society, life could be lived in a completely different way. 

The potential for an equal society—for socialism—already exists in capitalism, even if it is not always obvious. Fulfilling this potential is not a straightforward task, but it is an important and necessary one.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Victorian Liberals flag free speech crackdown
content:
State Liberal leader Jess Wilson has used a book launch to make public her intent to ban protests and political phrases in Victoria if elected in November. 

Speaking

 in Caulfield at the launch of 

Bondi Terror

, written by a SkyNews host and Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive officer Alex Ryvchin, Wilson 

linked

author: Lance Selfa
title: Trumpism swamped at the ballot box
content:
The US midterm elections were a stunning rebuke to President Trump and the Republican Party.

Votes are still being tallied around the country. But the extent of the Democratic Party’s victory is becoming clear. In Congress, Democrats will take office in January 2027 with majorities in both houses that were at the upper end of expectations before the election.

In fact, the national popular vote margin in favour of the Democrats is the largest since the mid-1970s Watergate era, and Democrats could end up with as many as 56 (of 100) senators, up from their current number of 47. That would be the largest Senate majority of either party since 2009. Media estimates predict a House majority of at least 250 Democrats (of 435 House members). That would be the largest House majority for either party since the early 1990s.

Democrats won Senate seats in longtime conservative Republican strongholds like Kansas (which hadn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932), Texas and South Carolina. Democrats made gains in every demographic group and region, compared to Kamala Harris’s performance in the 2024 presidential election.

In 2024, Harris lost a close race to Trump largely because, as the incumbent vice president, she carried the can for the Biden administration’s inability to tackle the inflation eroding working-class living standards. Key to Trump’s victory was his ability to add small, but significant, numbers of inflation-strapped voters among young people and people of colour (especially Latinos) to his “base” of white, middle-class Christian conservatives.

But Trump’s policies—from his erratic tariffs to the war against Iran, to huge cuts to medical assistance to fuel tax cuts to the rich—worsened the ability to afford necessities. What’s more, the administration’s unleashing of camouflaged thugs to arrest, imprison and deport hundreds of thousands of immigrants outraged millions. Democrats also tapped into disgust with the open corruption of Trump and his cronies, along with their disdain for the struggles of ordinary people.

The impact of these Trump actions repulsed all the groups who took a chance on Trump in 2024. Going into the 2026 midterms, opinion polls showed Trump to be the most unpopular president since Harry S. Truman in 1946. So, a pro-Democratic “wave” election wasn’t really in doubt. The question was how high the wave would be when it crested.

As has happened historically, Democratic gains rode atop a surge of Black (and more recently, Latino) voters. After the Supreme Court eviscerated the Voting Rights Act last summer, many civil rights advocates feared the return to political Jim Crow and a strengthening of one-party Republican rule in the southern states. But Black voters’ outrage expressed on 3 November had the impact of breaking through Republican domination in states like North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and even Mississippi.

In Texas, Latino voters forced a generational change and statewide sweep of the state that had become the cradle of post-civil-rights-era Republican politics. If the Republicans, as they are currently constituted, “lose” Texas, they will lose any sort of national political viability for a generation.

The 3 November results do not undermine the case for new civil rights and voting rights protections to undo the damage Trump and the Supreme Court have inflicted on the gains of the 1960s civil rights movement. But they show that breaking what former AFL-CIO political director Michael Podhorzer calls the “

Greater Confederacy

” is possible.

Trump and the Republicans had nothing positive to offer to voters. And they and their deep-pocketed donors spent billions attempting to excite their base with non-stop anti-trans and racist messaging against their Democratic opponents. Abdul el-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, took the full brunt of an Islamophobic campaign against him—not only from his Republican opponent, but also from pro-Israel Democratic Party politicians and operatives.

But all of this failed to rescue Republicans, even in their longtime strongholds. The voting majority rejected these “culture war” appeals, seeing them as deliberate attempts to distract from Republican malfeasance and catering to the rich. When all is said and done, Elon Musk will have figuratively lit half a billion dollars on fire.

It’s important to understand the election as a repudiation of Trump and Republican rule, not an endorsement of whatever it is the Democratic Party stands for. In many ways, and in many parts of the country, the electorate voted for progressive ballot measures. Voters in Missouri and Virginia codified abortion as a state constitutional right. Virginia voters ended the lifetime denial of voting rights to convicted felons and upheld same-sex marriage. In almost every locality where a moratorium or regulation on AI data centres—hated symbols of Big Tech oligarchs—was on the ballot, it passed.

But while the progressive tide on ballot measures was undeniable, it wasn’t universal. For example, some anti-trans measures passed, Idaho’s abortion ban remains in place, and Oklahoma elected a governor who wants to jail abortion patients. The proposed “billionaire’s tax” lost in California, mostly because many Democratic politicians opposed it.

And there is no denying the reactionary policies of some Democratic politicians, like Texas senator-elect James Talarico or Iowa senator-elect Josh Turek, who opportunistically threw trans people under the bus, or who insisted that they were for “border security”. That’s a reminder that while the Democrats may be the other option to the GOP on most ballots, 

they are not an opposition party

. The Democratic Party is a corporate-backed entity dedicated to supporting American capitalism and US empire.

Democrats campaigned on vague promises to bring “affordability” to ordinary Americans and “accountability” to the criminals in the Trump administration. But now that they have won congressional majorities, the voters who enabled those majorities will want to see real action. Half-hearted measures crafted to get around a Trump veto won’t suffice.

The corporate Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House in January, is already trying to soft-soap pledges to hold Trump and his minions accountable for corruption and law-breaking. Dems will also come under pressure not to “cut and run” from the Middle East if congressional majorities move to cut off funds for Trump’s war. Already, Big Tech is looking to hire Democrat-connected lobbyists to defend its interests on Capitol Hill.

The voters rejected what they saw as a corrupt status quo rigged in favour of a handful of billionaires and oligarchs. They are not looking for the Democrats to reconstruct that status quo on slightly more polite terms. If Democrats don’t realize that, they are setting themselves up for an even bigger defeat than 2024’s in the future.

One last point. When Trump came into office touting a mandate for a reordering of society along hard-right, ethnonationalist lines, about every major “liberal” institution capitulated to him. Law firms. Universities. Businesses that had touted their commitment to diversity. Even some labour unions, like the Teamsters. A considerable number of Democrats voted to support Trump’s program of mass arrests and deportations. For a few months, Trumpism appeared to be a juggernaut.

But ordinary people weren’t as cowed. Their bravery, particularly in organising to defend immigrants from raids in Los Angeles, Chicago and, most importantly, Minneapolis, gave confidence to millions. Minneapolis unions and activists mounted a mass political strike in January. Without these efforts to fight back against Trump’s depredations, his support would not have collapsed as rapidly or as thoroughly. No politician did that.

That will be an important lesson to remember in what will continue to be a long struggle to send Trumpism into the dustbin of history.

First published at the 

International Socialism Project

.

author: Vinil Kumar
title: Western Sydney Airport is a gift to business
content:
It’s rare for aviation executives and prime ministers to party in Western Sydney. But the opening of Sydney’s second airport, Western Sydney International (WSI), was an unmissable photo opportunity. Attendees included Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, his predecessors Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison, Jetstar CEO Stephanie Tully and NSW Premier Chris Minns. 

After the first passenger flight departed, the exodus back to the leafy Eastern Suburbs began, leaving behind the roar of turbo-fan engines that will only grow more frequent once the fanfare around the airport subsides.

The new airport is a monument to twenty-first century capitalism: a feat of human ingenuity, subordinated to corporate interests, with working-class people paying the price.

Background

Sections of business have long campaigned for a second major airport in Sydney. 

The established Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport at Mascot is boxed in by residential suburbs and Botany Bay. A third runway was opened in 1994, but community protests won a night-time curfew and hourly flight limits. 

Aviation is central to supply chains and corporate Australia wanted a new airport with minimal restrictions on its use.

After 60 years of 

proposals, disputes and false starts

, the project was revived in 2012, with the release of the Joint Study on Aviation Capacity in the Sydney Region by the federal and New South Wales governments. Its co-authors included the incoming Business Council of Australia head, Jennifer Westacott. 

The 

report

 warned Kingsford Smith airport would reach capacity by 2027 and unmet passenger and freight demand could cost as much as $60 billion by 2060. It argued the curfew “creates impediments for night-time movements of freight”, but that “an opportunity exists for a 24-hour freight facility to be established at a secondary airport”. Proximity to future warehousing and distribution centres made Western Sydney an enticing option.

Although the proposal for an airport at Badgerys Creek was rejected by the state and federal governments at the time, the 

Daily Telegraph

 immediately launched a 

renewed campaign

 for one. It was joined in its 

lobbying

 by the National Australia Bank, Harvey Norman, Crown Resorts, Channel 7 and executives from Western Sydney University. Backing was also 

secured

 from the peak body of local councils in Sydney. 

The Sydney Business Chamber, Western Sydney, led by former Labor state minister and member for Granville David Borger, 

established the Western Sydney Airport Alliance

 to cohere a local campaign for the airport.

In 2014, Liberal Prime Minister Tony Abbott’s federal cabinet approved the proposal for an airport at Badgerys Creek.  

Local residents objected. “Well, it’s going to make Western Sydney a nightmare to live in”, Geoff Brown, a 40-year resident of Penrith and member of the Western Sydney Conservation alliance, 

told the ABC

 at the time. “Growth and a fair go for Western Sydney doesn’t mean trashing the place, doesn't mean turning it into a wasteland of factories and industrial sites”, he said.

Abbott’s successor, Malcolm Turnbull 

manoeuvred

 to make the new airport a government-run project. The state and federal governments provided 

$29 billion in public funding

. Meanwhile Western Sydney’s hospitals, schools and public housing continued to crumble.

Government control enabled a grander development plan, including the construction of a new CBD around the airport, 

Bradfield City

. Part of Bradfield City’s purpose is military support, by “strengthening the defence industrial base through advanced manufacturing and semiconductor packaging”. 

The government ensured businesses had direct input. “It’s not often you get to help design an airport from scratch,” former Qantas CEO Alan Joyce 

celebrated

 in 2019. WSI’s then-CEO 

warmly welcomed

 the freight industry: “Tell us what size facility you need, tell us what technology you want in it and how you want it designed to optimise your productivity”. Construction company Lendlease was another big winner, scoring a 

$644 million contract

 for the airport’s earth works.

Careful messaging trumpeted WSI’s economic benefits to a dubious public, while noise and environmental concerns were addressed through non-binding consultation. Naming the airport after Australia’s youngest female pilot, Nancy Bird Walton, and highlighting Indigenous culture and sustainability in its design, represented an attempt to further head off opposition. 

Today

Cargo operations at WSI commenced on 26 July, and passenger services on 25 October. From November, WSI will also take over Kingsford Smith’s night freight operations. By 2063, the airport is projected to service 82 million passengers annually, and have a second runway. 

Noise was already an issue by August.

Barry Garousse, whose family lives less than two kilometres from the new airport, told the ABC that he gets as little as two hours of 

uninterrupted sleep

 some nights. “[I] drive semi-trailers, heavy vehicles, which we gotta comply with fatigue laws. At the moment I don’t comply with fatigue laws,” he said. 

The government’s promised noise insulation program is limited to adjacent suburbs and won’t process applications until April next year.

In July, 

Sydney’s redesigned airspace

 came into effect, concentrating multiple flightpaths for both airports over Western Sydney, particularly between Parramatta and Penrith. More flights have been routed over the city's poorest areas, while fewer flights will pass over its richest.

Flight paths over Western Sydney after 9 July. Graphic by Vinil Kumar using Inequality Map from 

OpenStats.com.au

, and flight paths from wsiflightpaths.gov.au.

“Since August, it’s been giving us grief,” Gina, a St Mary’s resident, told 

Red Flag

. “[T]rying to sleep with an aeroplane every half hour is cooked.”

Aircraft noise poses numerous health risks. The UK-based Aviation Environmental Federation 

found

 exposure “can lead to short-term responses such as sleep disturbance, annoyance, and impairment of learning in children, and long-term exposure is associated with increased risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, heart attack, stroke and dementia.” 

It also poses a 

risk to nearby wildlife

, including a not-for-profit animal sanctuary.

WSI’s noise abatement procedures “prefer” diverting night-time flights over the less-populated southwest approach—but only if conditions and flight numbers permit.

Traffic is also an issue—the airport’s train line won’t open until late 2027 or 2028. 

Instead, private bus services can charge 

up to $55 one way.

 Ubers cost 

even more

. A free shuttle bus from St Mary’s station runs every half hour, carrying 37 passengers per trip. It would take up to five buses with up to a two-hour wait to transport all 188 passengers on the first sold-out flight, assuming there’s no traffic. 

This was not an oversight: roads were prioritised. 

The initial plan in 2014 

did not include a rail link

, instead allocating $1.2 billion to upgrade major roads. The 2016 Airport Plan 

dismissed the need for rail services

 until “the mid-2040s”. Airport rail was only 

confirmed in 2018

 as part of a line for the new Western Sydney CBD. However, construction only began in 2022.

But 

freight was sorted by 2019

: “The airport’s freight precinct is set to have dedicated road access off the Northern Road, separating heavy vehicles from passenger traffic, which will enter the airport from the M12 on the opposite side of the site”.

Jet fuel will also be brought in by road

, using up to 65 B-double tankers per day at full capacity. A dedicated pipeline was investigated in 2024, but may not be “economically feasible” until the 2030s.

Safety

Capitalism’s drive to cut costs and intensify work also jeopardises industrial safety, including in aviation.

Multiple 

“near misses”

 at Kingsford Smith airport began the day after freight operations commenced at WSI, totalling eleven incidents by 31 August. 

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau’s 

preliminary report

 highlighted staff shortages, excessive workloads and noted controllers were “combining operational roles”, that is, doing two or more jobs at once.

Controllers had made 

anonymous complaints

 “regarding controller training, experience levels and overall preparation for the Sydney Basin airspace changes associated with the opening of the new Western Sydney International Airport”. 

To cut costs during the pandemic, the private operator of air traffic control services, Air Services Australia, offered early retirement to controllers more than 56 years old. This 

eliminated

 the most experienced 15 percent of its workforce. Recruitment has increased, but decades of experience can’t be replaced overnight.

Those holding the system together are working under pressure, with some working 

up to 800 hours of overtime per year, or working ten days straight on a regular basis

 according to the association representing controllers. 

But the bosses making decisions in corporate boardrooms are insulated from these problems. If anything, they’re determined to have fewer humans working in aviation.

WSI will be the first airport in Australia without a conventional control tower. Twenty-five cameras will feed video to a control centre seventeen kilometres away in Eastern Creek. 

Anonymous sources told the 

Sydney Morning Herald

 in August that 

low video quality

 required slowing flight movements as a precaution. Controllers couldn’t just look through binoculars or out the window to confirm aircraft positions. 

Loss of connectivity poses another risk. During 

April

 and 

September

, a remote control facility in Philadelphia lost radar around Newark Airport for more than a minute due to damaged cabling and backup systems failing. 

Some US airports have 

introduced AI systems

 to “advise” human controllers, with workers raising concerns about the reliability of summarised information and their ability to override AI guidance. 

 The politics of air travel

Working class people are locked out of decision making in capitalism. Democracy doesn’t extend to the workplace or the economy, including construction projects like WSI, Sydney’s toll roads, stadiums, countless luxury apartment blocks and data centres. 

The only way we can influence anything is collectively: campaigning, protesting and going on strike. Sydney Airport’s curfew, for example, was won through mass protest in the 1990s, including thousands rallying at Leichhardt oval and 

a 10,000-strong blockade of the airport

. This curfew was an important improvement in living standards for those living near the airport, which are not wealthy areas. 

Blockade of Sydney Airport on 17 December 1994. PHOTO: Photo: Brendan Esposito, Fairfax Archives.

The health and lives of western Sydney residents matter as much as anyone else’s. Demanding a curfew and 

compensation

, as was paid to residents near Kingsford Smith airport in the 1990s, should be the bare minimum. This will take serious public pressure and industrial muscle.

In recent months, 

hundreds of airport ground staff have struck

 to improve wages and conditions, meaning safer skies for everyone. Flight disruptions showed the potential power aviation workers have. 

Aviation has helped make satisfying human need possible by moving resources and people around the world at unprecedented speed. But capitalism’s profit-driven logic limits the possibilities. In a socialist society, where workers democratically control the economy, safety and sustainability would be prioritised over profit. 

Airports could be built away from cities, connected by rapid transit. Planned production could reduce excess flights from competing airlines, 

empty flights

 and unnecessary business travel. Destructive industries that add to travel volume, like the military, could and should be abolished Homes surrounding airports could be designed or upgraded with the best possible noise insulation. 

But capitalism will not forgo profits just so people can live decent lives. To win anything, from a decent night’s sleep to a decent society, we’ll need to fight them together and make a lot of noise of our own.

author: Jerome Small
