title: Debt angst is class war
content:
A flood of water, meant to symbolise debt, flows from the Victorian parliament, inundating suburban streets and living rooms while a scared child watches on. AI-generated ads like this, sponsored by right-wing outfit Fix Victoria, will be familiar to anyone in the state. 

Overwhelmingly, the media narrative is that Australia in general and Victoria in particular is drowning in debt. We’re told there’s no choice except brutal cuts to health, education, and other government spending. 

This is a powerful narrative, but a false one. 

It is being used by the ruling class to force workers to accept cuts, and to attack Labor governments federally and in Victoria. Labor is already bowing to this pressure by implementing cuts to vital services and implementing sharp cuts to real wages, except where union revolts threaten a crisis. 

Contrary to this right-wing myth, neither Victoria nor Australia is drowning in debt. Total government debt (combining both federal and state) has 

risen

 from 40 percent to 52 percent of gross domestic product over the past decade. But this level of debt is still relatively low by international standards—well below the UK (102 percent of GDP), Spain (97 percent), Canada (115 percent) and plenty of others. According to the International Monetary Fund, the “advanced economies” have an average government debt of 107% of GDP, more than double that of Australia.

Around the world, however, ruling class concern over debt levels—and who will pay that debt—has been sharpened by the sudden spike in global inflation and interest rates since mid-2021. The inflationary surge was fuelled initially by dislocations from the pandemic, and then by a series of “geopolitical shocks”—a euphemistic term for brutal imperialist wars—first Russia invading Ukraine in 2022, and more recently the US and Israel’s attack on Iran. These disrupted energy markets and pushed up the price of oil and gas, causing a global price shock. 

Surging demand for capital to fuel the AI bubble is also pushing global inflation and interest rates higher, as are rapidly expanding US deficits to fund Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and rearmament to prepare for war with China. 

None of these factors driving borrowing costs higher were created by working-class people, let alone by those of us who happen to live in Victoria. But around the world, and in every state, it’s working-class people who are expected to endure the increased cost of finance—through below-inflation wage rises, and by seeing vital services cut. 

In Victoria, Labor’s ambitious infrastructure agenda is at the centre of the right-wing campaign against the government. Initially, though, there was little serious ruling-class concern over this. 

Few disputed the need to update Melbourne’s rail infrastructure, or remove its plentiful level crossings. Melbourne still has nearly 

100

, despite the extensive program of removals, compared to just a 

handful

remaining in Sydney. Notably, removal of level crossings is a boon to road transport of all sorts—including major freight companies and small businesses, as well as commuters of all classes. 

Prior to Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel, the last major expansion of the city’s rail infrastructure was the City Loop, built under the state Liberal governments of the 1960s and 70s and opened by Labor in the early 1980s. And despite the river of anti-union propaganda about the construction unions, it's simply 

not the case

 that cost overruns on Victoria’s Big Build are substantially different to similar projects in New South Wales or elsewhere. 

Victoria is also far from the only state which financed infrastructure by taking out loans during a period of historically low interest rates. Victoria’s debt of $160 billion is 

higher

 than New South Wales at $117 billion, but both states have the same 

debt rating

 from international agencies—along with every Australian state except Western Australia, which enjoys massive royalty flows from iron ore and gas. Liberal and Labor governments in New South Wales in recent years found $65 billion for a series of massive new 

Metro rail projects

, $20 billion for the gigantic WestConnex tunnel, and a few billion here and there to help pay for a new international airport, a city tram system, and sundry other projects.

Former Premier Daniel Andrews’ approach to achieving its ambitious infrastructure agenda did not depend on increased taxes when it was launched. Instead, like similarly neoliberal governments around the world, Victorian Labor financed some of it through privatisations (notably the Port of Melbourne and VicRoads) and the rest from loans. The rail projects were an important part of Labor’s economic strategy, supposedly leading to increased land values and high-rise development, which would ultimately boost state government revenues. Everyone was a winner, it seemed.

This was uncontroversial at first. In 2016, the federal government could raise ten-year loans at interest rates as low as 2 percent, sinking to 1 percent in 2019. Even with the slight premium paid by state governments, a program of “borrow and spend”, as unapologetically advocated by Andrews, seemed a foolproof way to build long-overdue infrastructure and promote economic growth.  

That world is now gone. And the question of “who pays” has become a question of class power. 

By the end of 2022, central banks around the world were hiking interest rates at a rapid pace to combat rising inflation. It was clear from that point that 

a brutal reckoning

 for debtor states and companies was looming. 

Current economic orthodoxy states that any inflation above 2 or 3 percent per year—even if caused by “geopolitical shocks”—has to be countered by central banks raising interest rates. This cuts demand and, eventually, inflation. 

That this policy also risks mass unemployment and mass bankruptcies isn’t some mistake: it’s the point. One example of this brutal logic is the startlingly frank 

declaration

 by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Michele Bullock that one in 20 workers in Australia might have to be unemployed in order to depress demand enough to dent inflation. Interest rate rises also 

protect

 the enormous wealth of international finance at the expense of borrowers. 

Global pressures meant that by early 2022, the interest rate paid by the Australian government on a ten-year loan was over 3 percent: today, this rate is well over 5 percent. States pay slightly more, so refinancing costs for Victoria have jumped from close to 1 percent in 2019 to around 6 percent today.

So who will pay? Australia’s capitalist class wants workers to. 

Australian bosses have already achieved world-beating cuts to real wages, with the OECD 

reporting

 in July this year that though real wages have regained some of the lost ground in virtually all other “advanced” capitalist countries, “real wages are near the trough of the cost-of-living crisis only in New Zealand and Australia”. 

Victoria’s Labor government has done at least its share of the heavy lifting in this area. The string of drawn out, high-profile enterprise bargaining disputes this year—most notably involving school staff, but also tens of thousands of healthcare workers—has been fuelled by cuts to real wages of 11 percent for teachers,12 percent for many local council workers, 13 percent for allied health professionals, 14 percent for hospital orderlies, and 16 percent for medical scientists. These are extraordinary, life-altering cuts to living standards. These figures understate the hit to real wages for those with mortgages, which are not counted in the most common measure of inflation, the Consumer Price Index. 

Labor achieved this by imposing a below-inflation wage cap on public sector workers. Union leaders were initially successful in selling these wage cuts on behalf of their Labor pals, though repeated episodes of rank-and-file revolt since 2022 have led to several important fights. Some of these battles (especially by nurses, ambulance paramedics, school staff, and medical scientists) have resulted in wage rises that might remedy the real wage cut of recent years by 2028 or 2029 if inflation doesn’t keep accelerating. 

But even then, the tens of thousands of dollars lost to inflation over several years represents a substantial involuntary donation by working-class people to Victoria’s creditors—which include the wealthiest entities in the country and the world. Calculating this total vast transfer of wealth with any accuracy is a job that no journalist for the capitalist press seems to have gotten around to (in contrast to various made-up, hyperventilating estimates for the alleged cost of union wages on construction sites). For a very rough calculation, we can use a conservative 

estimate

 of $20,000 in total wages lost to inflation over the past four years by someone on the average wage. Multiplied across 320,000 Victorian public sector employees, we come to a rough figure of $6.4 billion since 2022. 

Labor has also raised money by introducing new taxes small-scale capitalists—for example a tax on Airbnb rentals which is 

reported

 to raise $86 million per year; a 2021 “premium” stamp duty on real estate sales over $2 million, which was 

planned

 to bring in $137 million per year; and a 2023 reduction on the threshold at which land tax becomes payable on second properties, 

stated

 to bring in around $1.2 billion per year. And to howls of protest from big business, the Victorian government also imposed payroll tax surcharges on the biggest companies, lifting the rate in Melbourne from 4.85 percent to 6.85 percent of payroll. These surcharges reportedly raise $2.2 billion per year—less than two percent of the state government’s $130 billion budget for this year. 

For the big capitalists, and the many small fry, these taxes are an offence against all that is holy. Cue AI-generated attack ads, reams of doomsday class war rhetoric in the pages of the 

Australian Financial Review

, and an entirely predictable capitulation from Labor. One part of this is Labor premier Ben Carroll 

announcing

the phased reversal of the changes to the land tax threshold by 2031 at a cost of $230 million over the next five years, part of the pre-election gallop to the right by an already thoroughly neoliberal Victorian Labor government. 

A more consequential move has been Labor’s dramatic and ongoing cuts to public sector jobs and programs, starting in 2023. The well-publicised “Silver Review” released last year, which recommended 1,000 public sector job cuts, is supposed to save $4 billion over the next four years. 

But this is just the tip of the iceberg. The entire Victorian public sector is effectively in the grip of a giant continuous restructuring and downsizing exercise. Most of these cuts fly under the radar, apart from the occasional ones made an issue by workers, unions and concerned others. These include the planned destruction of 

VicHealth

 (Victoria’s only public health promotion agency), cuts to the beloved 

State Library of Victoria,

 and the 

abolition

 of a program which helps new parents learn how to settle their babies. 

This will accelerate under a Liberal government. The Liberals have publicly declared they will not fill vacancies in the public service for four years if elected in November. This will have a devastating effect across every government service.

Labor is paving their way. Every week brings news of fresh cuts, like that to 

disability inclusion funding

 in Victorian schools, or long-term underfunding, such as the 

news

 that a third of the new Footscray hospital is empty because of a lack of funding for staff. Then there are the big announcements which turn out to mean nothing much, such as the recent announcement of a supposed path to so-called “full” funding for Victoria’s government schools. A look at the 

detail

 shows this announcement fails to increase funding in real terms by even one full percentage point over the next four years.

Despite a few minor gestures to cost-of-living relief here and there, and some relatively minor taxes on business, the largest part of Labor’s plan to appease the gods of the financial markets is to impose austerity on those of us least able to afford it. 

Of course, this is not the only course available. 

Victorian Socialists’ policies 

include

 some straightforward measures to raise revenue, such as ending Crown Casino’s one-dollar-per-year peppercorn rent on their massive Southbank site, imposing a 10 percent wealth tax on billionaires’ assets, and further increases on payroll tax for large companies. These and other measures, to quote the VS program, “should be used to push towards a socialised and democratic economy that works in the interests of the majority”. 

A step towards that would be seriously taxing the super-rich. The wealth of the country’s richest 200 people more than tripled in the past decade, from $197 billion in 

2016

 to $707 billion in 

2026

. So there’s no shortage of wealth. There’s just a shortage of a mass working-class movement prepared to fight—industrially and politically—to reclaim the wealth that our labour produces. Our task is to build such a movement. 

Labor, Liberal or One Nation—or whatever toxic combination we end up with in Victoria—will cut vital services for workers and the poor, to supposedly fix the supposed “flood” of debt. Whoever ends up in power, working-class people will have a hell of a fight on our hands.

author: Shirley Killen
title: Inside the Victorian Socialists’ Footscray campaign
content:
There’s something special about the Victorian Socialists’ campaign in the inner-west Melbourne seat of Footscray. On almost every front, the campaign leads the way state-wide: number of doors knocked, yard signs delivered, volunteers involved. In an election overshadowed by rising far-right influence and a right-wing shift, Footscray reveals a base for radical left politics.

This month, I spent some time with the Footscray crew, talking to locals at the AFLW matches at Whitten Oval, and sitting down with candidate Jasmine Duff to figure out the magic behind this campaign.

Jas starts by painting a picture of the electorate she’s fighting to represent: “Footscray has the progressive social conscience of Brunswick, but class questions are shoved in people’s faces way more”.

Melbourne’s inner-west is full of young workers and renters, people who care about questions like climate change and Indigenous justice. Residents value the community's diversity, enjoying the pubs, gigs, and local footy—during the AFLW Pride round in early October, many Bulldogs fans mentioned that they supported VS and some signed up to host a yard sign. It shares this sensibility with other parts of the city where Victorian Socialists has built a serious foothold, like Brunswick and Northcote.

But in Footscray, deep class inequality is an indelible part of the social fabric, and the effects of poverty and for-profit development are impossible to ignore. Homelessness and drug use are more visible than in many other parts of Melbourne; old buildings sit empty and derelict while landowners wait for gentrification to increase property values.

Footscray’s population will grow in the next ten years, yet infrastructure and social services are failing to meet the rising demand. More investment is desperately needed in health care, mental health and public housing. But state Labor governments have run down these services even further over many years, turning instead to more policing to punish vulnerable people. 

This has created a sense that Footscray faces conflicting pressures. The state government is keen to entice private developers to build on the 22 inner-city sites currently being land-banked—but to do that, they have to show that property values are increasing, and that means cracking down on rough sleeping and crime. And the community is divided: there is a strong right-wing current, protesting against crime and targeting migrants.

But there’s a different vision for Footscray, too—one that prioritises high-quality public housing, green spaces, public transport and wraparound services to meet the needs of ordinary people. One that argues that vacant sites such as Forges, the old Footscray Hospital and Little Saigon ought to serve the public interest rather than developers’ profits. Initiatives such as The People’s Plan for Footscray highlight this alternative vision and overlap with Victorian Socialists’ demands.

An important aspect of Footscray is that left-wing and progressive people don’t just settle for wishful thinking about improving their communities, they fight for change. Last year, when Victoria Police killed Somali man Abdifatah Ahmed in the heart of Footscray CBD, hundreds rallied to call for justice. Countless local campaign groups are working on issues such as pollution, green spaces, transport, and opposing the huge data centres sprouting up across the west.

Recently, local legends in Yarraville struck a significant blow to data centre giant NextDC, inspiring thousands worldwide who are challenging tech giants in their communities. NextDC is attempting to expand its West Footscray data centre complex, despite serious local opposition. To do this, they must build 22-metre steel power poles (twice the usual height) along residential streets to provide the centre with the vast amount of electricity needed for its operation. 

When electricity provider Jemena sent a construction crew to erect these poles, locals blocked the work in whatever ways they could—parking cars in the way of machinery, putting wheelie bins out on the street and refusing to answer their doors to the work crew. This heartening expression of collective resistance forced Jemena to retreat. Even sweeter was the immediate hit to NextDC’s margins caused by the delay—the company’s shares 

plummeted by 40 percent

 and it lost around $3 billion in valuation.

Jas says that many of the people leading this campaign have a Victorian Socialists yard sign displayed on their front fence. The party’s project to confront profit-hungry corporations wrecking our communities has resonated with individuals fighting the good fight, spanning from the largest nationwide campaigns to the battles we face in our own front yards.

The Footscray campaign has brought together individual socialists who had not found their place in politics before. Jas tells me about those who visit the Victorian Socialists volunteer centre on Paisley Street. They come for the weekly Tuesday night working bees, to collect a yard sign, or simply to find out what the campaign involves. They might start off feeling they have nothing much to offer, yet after a chat and lingering for a while beyond the time they planned, they go away taking responsibility for a small section of the work.

Some people show up at the volunteer centre to get involved because they’ve read a leaflet dropped on their doorstep and immediately identify with the radical worldview of the Socialists. One couple collected a yard sign and took a list of orders to drop off nearby. Now they have a group chat with the other socialists on their street, where they can organise letterboxing and other local campaigning. Leaning into this localised organising has proved to be a strength of the Footscray campaign, providing easy avenues for newcomers to learn how to campaign.

Dedicated people like these can’t easily be put back in their box. Whatever the result come 28 November, the socialist movement in Footscray is here to stay.

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The return of left-wing parties
content:
The downfall of powerful leaders, the implosion of establishment parties, the rapid rise of far-right demagogues and the eruption of economic crises have become regular features of twenty-first century capitalism. The ensuing accumulation of discontent has in turn repeatedly triggered mass protests, riots and rebellions, such as those currently unfolding in Spain and France. The challenge for socialists today is to transform these explosions of discontent into durable, mass socialist organisations.

For decades, significant sections of the radical left were deeply sceptical about organisation building. Social democracy’s embrace of neoliberalism and the collapse of Stalinism seemed to discredit the idea. The emphasis shifted to horizontal organising, the valorisation of leaderlessness and a liberal version of anarchism.

In the early 2010s, the pendulum swung back a bit. The rise of SYRIZA in Greece and Podemos in Spain embodied this trend, with both new left parties arising from mass anti-austerity struggles. Their initial success inspired similar attempts in other advanced capitalist countries.

This immediately raised questions about what kind of socialism these new parties advocated—or whether socialism was their goal at all. Though breaking with moderate centre-left politics, they frequently replicated the reformist politics and practices of older left-wing parties, with predictable results.

In July 2015, for example, SYRIZA Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras capitulated to European creditors, accepting a harsh bailout and stricter austerity just days after Greek voters rejected them in a landslide 61 percent popular vote against such measures. Podemos, having condemned traditional political elites and media bosses as “la casta”, entered a coalition with the centre-left Socialists in 2020, abandoning its anti-austerity platform and accepting the repression of the Catalan independence movement. By the early 2020s, most of these new left parties had stagnated, plunged into internal crises, or collapsed.

In the US, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) membership fell from 93,000 in 2021 to under 60,000 by 2024, alongside a growing sense of aimlessness. This decline was driven by critical support for Joe Biden’s administration—defending Biden even as his own party turned on him. Aligned figures like Bernie Sanders and “the Squad” shifted rightward, with 

Jacobin

 writer Branko Marcetic noting in 2023 that the Squad went from being leftist darlings to targets denounced as “sellouts” and “warmongers”.

Germany’s Die Linke faced a profound crisis in 2023 and 2024 after top politician Sahra Wagenknecht left to form a rival party; polling dropped to 3 percent and tens of thousands left the movement. La France Insoumise (LFI), led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, faced similar challenges: its presidential vote share fell from 19.58 percent to 10 percent between 2019 and 2021, membership dropped to 300,000, and its deputies lacked political clarity.

Today, however, the landscape has changed yet again. The DSA has now surpassed 120,000 members, securing key electoral wins including six members of Congress post-midterms, strong representation in New York alongside Mayor Mamdani, and 50 state legislators nationwide.

Die Linke experienced an even sharper revival. After surging to 8.8 percent in the February 2025 elections, membership doubled to 123,000. It now leads in Berlin and among voters under 30, and in August it overtook the SPD nationally for the first time, polling more than 12 percent.

In France, LFI may well end up in a presidential run-off against the far-right National Rally (RN). Holding 71 deputies and 500,000 members under a younger leadership generation, LFI has eclipsed traditional centre-left parties. Elsewhere, Belgium’s Workers’ Party (PTB-PVDA) expanded to 25,000 members and 15 MPs, while Austria’s Communist Party (KPÖ) dominates Graz and is rising in other urban centres.

The membership of these parties is less active and politically developed than the memberships of the mass socialist and communist parties of the past. And there are important exceptions where the situation is much less favourable: initially promising attempts to launch Your Party in the UK stalled disastrously, Greek leftists still struggle with SYRIZA’s legacy and Spanish social democrats reclaimed support during Podemos’s crisis.

Nonetheless, mass left-wing parties with tens of thousands of members are now permanent fixtures across many advanced capitalist countries. The compounding crises of modern capitalism—COVID-19, Gaza, the rise of Trump and the far right, inequality, AI threats, and imperialist conflict—have expanded the audience for the left.

This revival has also been aided by some parties adopting greater organisational and ideological seriousness, embedding themselves in movements, and in some cases shifting to the left.

Two examples are worth looking at in more detail. 

The first is Die Linke. Following Sahra Wagenknecht’s 2023 departure, Die Linke revived itself by building chapters rooted in working-class communities, local party organisers, recruiting activists, and mass door-knocking campaigns.

Despite initial scepticism, this strategy laid the foundation for the party’s 2025 revival, supported by educational programs from the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung. Die Linke also sank strong roots into anti-fascist movements against the far-right Alternative for Germany, recruiting heavily on campuses and high schools to support left-wing candidates like Ferat Koçak in Berlin. Left currents like Marx21 led these protests, providing a bridge into party membership. 

On Palestine, however, Die Linke clings to liberal Zionist politics. Despite internal pressure from its youth wing and left branches, the leadership has repeatedly suppressed solidarity events, prompting a public fallout with the LFI after they cancelled a Berlin meeting with LFI parliamentarian and Gaza Flotilla participant Emma Fourreau. Younger members push for pro-Palestine politics while older leaders resist.

The second is LFI. Under Jean-Luc Mélenchon, La France Insoumise established the Institut La Boétie in 2019 to address political weaknesses. Modelled on historical Communist Party schools, it offers rigorous training courses in historical materialism, eco-socialism, and techno-feudalism for deputies and candidates, as well as functioning as a research hub.

It has undergone a dramatic political transformation from an electoral shell into a mass party embedded in grassroots activism. Mélenchon forged ties with militant anti-fascist groups like Jeune Garde, and its elected representatives now come directly from strike committees and anti-racist movements rather than traditional political circles.

Politically, Mélenchon and LFI shifted leftward on French nationalism, Islamophobia and Palestine—opposing racist policing, championing anti-militarist and anti-NATO actions, and positioning the party as the most popular left force in France’s working-class and migrant suburbs.

Despite their revitalisation though, these parties have not radically broken with their past politics, and revolutionary critiques from the 2010s remain relevant. Their strategic shift—pioneered by Belgium’s PTB-PVDA—emphasises long-term organisation over rushing into power behind charismatic leaders in response to the failures of SYRIZA, Podemos and former UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. However, this shift is largely pragmatic and leaves fundamental political problems unquestioned.

The DSA remains trapped within the Democratic Party—one of the most powerful capitalist institutions in the world. Its elected representatives have repeatedly sought to play nice with party powerbrokers in order to avoid a serious confrontation. There is no plan to build an independent party. Consequently, DSA’s “democratic socialism” aligns closer to left liberalism than European left parties. Should Democrats return to the White House in 2028, these tensions will re-emerge as in the Biden years.

In Europe, left parties face structural crossroads. For Die Linke, the central issue remains its willingness to enter coalition governments with neoliberal parties. Bodo Ramelow in Thuringia raised the possibility of a coalition with the centre-right Christian Democrats. Following the Berlin state elections, coalition negotiations began between Die Linke, the Greens and the SPD. Die Linke’s leadership signed a provisional agreement excluding party members who support BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) or reject Israel’s right to “defend itself”.

There has been opposition to this agreement by sections of the Die Linke membership. One hundred and twenty elected politicians and party officials have signed a statement condemning it. However, even critics of the agreement accept the idea that forming a coalition government with the SPD and the Greens is desirable. This is despite the fact that the Greens are a neoliberal pro-war middle-class party, far to the right of the Australian Greens, while the SPD has followed the same path as the ALP, embracing cuts to social spending, privatisations and tax cuts for the wealthy. The only way Die Linke can form a government with these parties is by compromising its minimum program of significantly expanding publicly owned housing. And Die Linke has a long history of being involved in compromised coalition state governments across Germany, with frankly little to show for it.

If Mélenchon won the French presidency, the country would not be on the road to socialism. Beneath all the rhetoric about ending Western civilisation and starting fresh with a new political and economic model, Mélenchon’s vision is a reformed capitalism. He argues for the creation of a Sixth Republic based on a new constitution that would dilute the centralised power of the French president, shift governance towards a parliamentary system and create more space for popular referendums and citizen councils. LFI’s economic program includes raising the minimum wage, increasing taxes on the rich and expanding public ownership, but it does not call for the expropriation of the banks or large businesses. Mélenchon argues that France should leave NATO and break any military ties with the US and Israel. But he also argues for expanding the French military, is ambiguous on whether French imperialism can play a progressive role in Africa and argues for restructuring, but not abolishing, the police. 

The immediate issue that would be raised by Mélenchon’s presidency is whether he could break with the neoliberal economic and political model that has dominated the Western world for decades. Mélenchon argues that his presidency will be different from previous failed attempts, because his government would not back down in the face of capitalist panic. He claims that he would introduce strict regulation of capital movement and financial markets, including public control over key banking channels if necessary. He also argues that his party would only come to power on the back of widespread social unrest and popular mobilisations, which would force the French ruling class to begrudgingly compromise with his presidency.

It is hard not to be sceptical about this. The French ruling class, backed by the rest of the European establishment, will unleash everything they have to stop any attack on their wealth. While Mélenchon has embraced mass protest to a greater extent than other reformist leaders, LFI is still primarily electoral in its focus. His vision of a “citizen’s revolution” is a peaceful election of an LFI government that will shake things up by mobilising people in mass rallies and referendums, but will not empower the working class to wage war against the capitalist system. 

In countries where left parties are large, the revolutionary left faces tough decisions about how to relate to these forces and their followers. Working out how to avoid abandoning revolutionary politics for reformism, without alienating workers and students influenced by the new left parties, is a real challenge.

What is certain is that this phenomenon can’t be ignored. The growing recognition of the need to be organised is a step in the right direction. Revolutionaries need to find a way to use these developments to win a new generation to organising to overthrow capitalism.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Community resistance kneecaps data centre in Melbourne’s west
content:
Data centre construction and AI development is fuelling the global economy. In Australia, there are more than 200 data centres at various stages of development or construction. The tech industry’s restructuring of our lives, neighbourhoods and environment can feel like an unstoppable force, pushing aside anything standing in the way of huge profits and industry dominance. 

This is not happening without resistance though, and sometimes, despite the odds, this resistance has an impact. 

The residents of West Footscray are one such example. The enemy they were up against was NextDC, a multi-billion dollar company and the largest developer and operator of data centres in Australia. 

In 2021, NextDC built its M3 data centre with approval from the state government. Local residents complained about disruptive construction, diesel fuel pollution, noise from the centre’s operation and interference with their energy supply. One woman, speaking to a Victorian Socialists campaigner, described losing power to her house—an annoyance for most people but potentially catastrophic for her family, as one member requires constant access to a dialysis machine.

NextDC applied to the state government in February to expand its M3 data centre, with a decision expected next year. To achieve the requested upgrades, the centre needs significantly more power than it currently has access to. The old wooden power poles and existing power lines in the surrounding area, designed for residential homes, aren’t going to cut it. According to the 

Sydney Morning Herald

, these only carry 400 volts, whereas 66,000 volts are needed to power the proposed expanded data centre.

Without warning or consultation, and without the expansion even being approved, huge 22-metre high power poles nevertheless started going up in West Footscray in September, replacing the modest wooden poles people are used to. Residents were rightly outraged. Many of them had previously been involved in campaigning against NextDC and the M3 data centre. They were already connected via social media, had been in contact with the mainstream media and had organised protests and community outreach events. A protest against the centre’s expansion in early August, called by a community meeting organised by Victorian Socialists’ Jorge Jorquera (a former Maribynong councillor), attracted more than 150 people in the pouring rain. When construction began then, residents were in a position to take action quickly. 

Coordinating with their neighbours, the guerrilla rebels of West Footscray parked their cars over construction work, filled holes with rubbish and green waste, and collectively refused to answer their doors to construction workers. 

Their actions caused such a stir, as well as delays to the poles going up, that the council brokered an end to the work with Jemena, the company responsible for the power poles and lines. On 31 August Jemena stopped works and on 24 September the Maribyrnong council put out a statement saying that works to the power supply for the data centre would remain paused.

Those of us watching along speculated about what would happen next. We heard whispers that they might continue work to boost the centre’s power supply, possibly using underground power cables, a much more costly option.

What we didn’t expect was the announcement from NextDC a month later that it was pausing trading of its stocks, due to “construction delays”. When trading resumed, the stock plunged by 40 percent in one day, cutting $3 billion off the company’s market valuation. NextDC bosses had planned to go to their next board meeting to 

request an increase to their pay

, but since the West Footscray debacle they are now proposing a 10 percent pay cut for directors, the board chairman is standing down and NextDC CEO Craig Scroggie is losing several million dollars’ worth of bonuses. The company is also likely to face a 

class action

 on behalf of shareholders because of this mismanagement. 

The residents of West Footscray are not outliers. Local communities have successfully campaigned against the building of data centres in 

Katoomba

 and 

Lane Cove

 in New South Wales and 

Greensquare

 in Western Australia. Politicians had previously declared Australia open for business for data centre companies. But in late October, the Municipal Association of Victoria, the peak body for councils in Victoria, passed a motion at its state council meeting demanding the state government impose an immediate moratorium on the construction of new data centres, and the federal Labor government has announced it intends to introduce restrictions on where data centres can be built. 

The backlash is significant enough that it is causing companies to consider relocating their operations. According to the 

Australian Financial Review

, Microsoft and NextDC representatives told the New South Wales government that “projects would move to Malaysia or Indonesia—where there are also substantial tax incentives and financial support—if they were unable to lock in power agreements or navigate a complex planning system”. 

The 

Australian Financial Review

 is not happy about the potential for hippies and homeowners acting together to stop these evil tech companies. An opinion piece in October declared that “[b]locking progress because of power poles or even copyright concerns is a mismeasure of the moment we are in. There are ways of solving the problems before us, but they shouldn’t stall our ability to be world-leading. The challenge is more than seeing off data centre activists, we can’t just run on a defensive footing. We need to play offence too.”

Its author, Lidija Ivanovski, argues that data centres are central to “Australian industry, defence and the economy”. Unfortunately for her and her tech bro buddies, regular people care more about the environment, cost of living and quality of life than the power and sophistication of the Australian military. Nor does the West Footscray community care about mollifying big data construction companies—they saw something they didn’t like and decided to act, and in so doing demonstrated the power ordinary people can have against these behemoths. 

There are still dozens of data centres being built or seeking approval across the country. Hopefully more community resistance erupts in response, and reminds us of the power we have when we act together.

author: Omar Hassan
title: Ben Carroll’s ‘new direction’ for Victoria is towards the big end of town
content:
In his first statement released following the ousting of Jacinta Allan, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll promised “a new direction” for Victoria. So far, it’s been the longitudinal equivalent of prostrating yourself at the feet of the bosses and hoping for a better ride in the media. And it doesn’t feel that new.

Granted, Carroll came to office more determined than Allan to concede to each and every one of the right-wing attacks on the Labor government. He has distanced himself from the Big Build, and immediately announced a royal commission into the CFMEU, the key demand of the bosses and right wing who see an opportunity to strike a blow against unionism.

Carroll has also announced a softening of the land tax changes introduced by former premier Daniel Andrews, one of the few progressive taxation policies introduced in recent years. This is a signal to business and the wealthy that a Carroll government will not be expecting them to make sacrifices to reduce the state’s debt. 

But on many other issues, Carroll is more of the same. Crime is an example. The capitalist media’s constant focus on incidents of anti-social behaviour has created the impression that Victorians are living in an era of unprecedented violence and crime. Yet the crime rate is 

roughly the same

 as it was a decade ago, according to data drawn from the Victorian Crime Statistics Agency. 

Nevertheless, Caroll has announced a “zero tolerance” approach to crime, involving “less bail, more jail”. Not satisfied with their draconian “adult time for adult crime” laws introduced by Allan which target children as young as 13, Labor has promised a review aimed at legislating harsher sentences for young offenders. His government has also committed $150 million in new funding for expanded police and PSO numbers. The latter are being empowered to patrol in wider areas, including shopping malls.

Police are also being given the right to frisk people for knives anywhere at any time, despite a 2022 Griffith University review into a similar law in Queensland finding that there was “

no evidence

” that it deterred knife carrying or led to a reduction in violent offending. What the policy will definitely achieve is to expand the systematic harassment of youths from poor and migrant backgrounds.

To the extent there are real issues with anti-social behaviour and crime, much of it is driven by poverty, the housing crisis and lack of social services. According to the Council for Homeless Persons (CHP), the homeless population rose by 24 percent in the five years to 2021, the last census for which data is available. The perpetrators of this invisible crime are the developers and the banks, but most of all the Labor government, which is responsible for Victoria having the lowest proportion of public and community housing in Australia. The CHP also reported that the Victorian government slashed spending on social housing by 9 percent in the 2024–25 budget, despite having the largest number of people seeking emergency housing support. 

The Labor government is also demolishing every public housing tower in the city to make way for private development on lucrative inner-city land. The residents of these buildings have largely been dispersed to the outer suburbs, where housing is cheaper and services are woefully inadequate. 

In a similar vein, the government has failed to address the ballooning numbers of people seeking support in dealing with drug and alcohol problems. In May, the Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association reported there were 5,122 Victorians on daily waitlists for drug treatment services, a 115 percent increase since the pandemic. These are people who are actively seeking support, but 40 percent had not even been assessed. 

Insofar as there is youth crime, it can’t be separated from the conditions of life for many young people, and in particular the condition of schools. Too many, especially those in poor areas, are not adequately resourced, particularly when it comes to assisting students with special needs. It is a disgrace that we still lack full-time professional social workers and counsellors in every public school, and that it is incredibly difficult to get funding for support staff in classrooms without a disability diagnosis. The government prefers to lock kids up rather than support them to get an education.

Faced with these issues, the obvious answer is to increase funding to assist people in acute situations to find shelter, health care, job and educational opportunities and financial assistance. 

There are a handful of measures that aim to sweeten the otherwise bitter pill. The establishment of ten public, walk-in dental clinics across the state is one. The proposal to cap fees for toll roads and public transport fees to $30 a day is another. While superficially attractive, this is essentially a $300 million a year taxpayer subsidy to Metro and the toll companies—socialists call for both to be renationalised without compensation. Labor has also promised to provide free abortion care on demand, a relatively cheap and very overdue measure, likely to cost just $7.5 million a year. None of this will fundamentally address cost-of-living issues for working-class people. 

Wage rises, which 

would

 make a significant difference to the standard of living of hundreds of thousands of Victorians, are not on offer from this government. Teachers, health workers and doctors have been denied their pay demands by the Carroll government, and it has maintained the 3 percent wage cap for public sector workers, which is well below the rate of inflation. 

Overall, Labor’s response to the surge in support for One Nation and growing support for the Liberals has been to attempt to curry favour with the bosses while throwing some crumbs at its base. The capitalist establishment is far from convinced, and is clearly all-in on a Liberal victory come November. Yet the effect of Carroll’s approach means that whoever wins, Victorian workers face an extended period of reactionary law and order policies, declining living standards and reduced investment into public services.

author: Editors
title: Turmoil in world politics: we have to rise to the challenges
content:
“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times ... it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.” The famous opening words of Charles Dickens novel, 

A Tale of Two Cities,

 set in the Great French Revolution could equally apply to France and much of Europe today.

The best of times and spring of hope—the vibrant, months-long school student mobilisations and blockades that have drawn hundreds of thousands of French workers and university students onto the streets in solidarity. All in the face of savage police violence unleashed by President Emmanuel Macron’s government of the supposed moderate liberal centre.

Eventually, after weeks of foot-dragging, trade union leaders called a general strike for 5 November—a vital step forward and test for the rebellion.

It is not just France. A wave of protest inspired by the French students has swept Europe from Belgium to Portugal to Italy, where students and workers have long endured similar attacks on living standards and democratic rights, the rise of militarism and threatening fascist forces.

Spain has also been gripped by revolt over the cost of living and housing crisis sparked by the eviction of 87-year-old woman Maricarmen Abascal. The general strike called for 11 November is set to be the largest in Spain in the 50 years since the fall of General Franco’s fascist government.

But it’s also the worst of times—reflected in the scale of support for far-right forces internationally.

The majority of the French population sympathises with the protestors’ grievances over the cost-of-living, cuts to public services and education funding. Yet polls indicate Marine Le Pen of the fascist National Rally is set to decisively win April’s presidential elections. Le Pen leads the left’s Jean-Luc Melenchon 69 percent to 31 percent. 

Large sections of the capitalist class and its middle-class supporters are rallying behind National Rally as the “party of order” to crush resistance not just from unruly students but organised workers and impose harsh austerity measures to boost profits.

Similarly in Spain, the right-wing People’s Party backed by the fascist Vox seems set to defeat the discredited centre-left government in the 29 November elections on a program of wage cuts, mass public sector sackings and attacks on democratic rights.

Then there is Brazil. An inspiring wave of protests led by young people transformed the course of the elections ensuring the defeat of the far right’s Flavio Bolsonaro. Yet the increasingly violent far right shows no sign of being curbed. Ruling in the interests of Brazil’s capitalist class, Lula da Silva’s Workers Party disillusioned swathes of workers and the poor preparing the ground for the far right. And a re-elected Lula is not about to change course and mobilise workers in mass strike action to challenge the rich and powerful.

Politics worldwide has become much more polarised, the product of decades of neo-liberal attacks on workers’ living standards and increasingly authoritarian rule undermining the hold of parties of the centre-left and centre-right. The pattern is uneven, but in many countries it is the far right that so far has been the main beneficiary of the growing discontent.

From Spain to France to Germany to Australia, the traditional reformist parties have utterly failed to defend workers’ interests and ward off the far-right threat. It is vital that the militant socialist left and the broader working-class movement is rebuilt to meet these challenges. And there are important opportunities to do just that.

There is a much greater opening for Marxist, working-class politics than in previous waves of protests over the last few decades. In Spain, for example, the 2011 movement of the squares provoked by the 2008 Global Financial Crisis was posed as a citizens’ movement that was neither left nor right. There was pronounced hostility to the involvement of socialist organisations and trade unions.

This time around, the movement is much more posed as a movement of the left centred on working-class demands with the involvement of revolutionary organisations welcomed. Mass strike action by workers is rightly seen as vital for the movement going forward.

In France, it was students from the poorest working-class suburbs that initiated the rebellion and the party most associated with the rebellion is Melenchon’s left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI). 

But half-way house left reformist operations like Melenchon’s LFI or the Left Party in Germany, which do not want to overthrow capitalism, are not up to the tasks that the situation demands. The LFI to its credit defends the student protests but does not intervene as an organised force in the movement to take it forwards, nor does it galvanise its hundreds of thousands of supporters to agitate in the unions for strikes that go beyond a simple one-day affair.

Australia has lagged behind developments in Europe. But here too we see increasing discontent with the mainstream parties and the rapid rise in support for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. In Victoria, we are set to see the election of a hard right Liberal government, backed by One Nation, out to implement a raft of austerity measures attacking workers.

Our side needs to rise to the challenge. This serious situation demands both concerted mass resistance and the building of a revolutionary socialist movement that is determined to take the struggle against capitalism all the way.

author: Alma Torlakovic
title: Western Sydney residents in revolt after being kept in the dark over data centre
content:
In their rush to appease big tech billionaires and open up Australia as a destination for hyperscale data centres, Labor governments at all levels have demonstrated how little respect they have for the people living in their so-called “safe seats”. This is most obvious in the diverse communities of Western Sydney, where the state government has rushed to approve a dozen of these polluting, energy-intensive monstrosities.

Labor has relied on the same blueprint for each recent approval: declare the data centre as a “state significant development”, don’t let the residents know and hope that nobody checks the website for the development proposals. They have gone as far as overselling the projects on behalf of the companies, claiming that they will create jobs for the community, downplaying the hazards involved or regurgitating the idea that these are not much different from a storage warehouse.

This strategy has backfired in Guildford in Sydney’s western suburbs, where a community campaign is brewing over the state government’s approval of a $1.1 billion hyperscale data centre right next to a sports field and homes. Residents are outraged that they've been left in the dark about the 7.2-hectare data centre that will cause 24/7 noise, raise energy bills, emit carcinogenic fumes, lower people's house prices and have a huge impact on water usage and carbon emissions. We are determined to stop it, as other communities have.

An information session organised by Cumberland City Council on 24 October to address the growing community backlash to the project turned into an angry row as 100 local residents turned on council officials, the mayor and local Labor MP, Julia Finn. Residents accused them of leaving them in the dark about the project, with most only learning of the 68-megawatt data centre plans in their neighbourhood during the past fortnight. Finn, who claimed that letters had been sent to residents, was booed down by angry constituents who said that no such thing had happened.

Robyn Hann, who is spearheading the action group to stop the data centre build, said:

“We went to the [council] information session hoping to learn more and have our concerns addressed regarding health, water, pollution, 24/7 noise, house prices and other issues. Instead, we got smoke and mirrors … I felt we were completely ignored.”

One woman summed it up, telling the meeting that she had lived in the area and worked hard for 30 years to pay off her home and build a life, only to be blindsided by this project.

Western Sydney residents are sick and tired of being taken for granted by the Labour Party and being the dumping ground for polluting industries. I have published a 

petition

 to demand that the Cumberland City Council and the NSW government put an immediate stop to this project. It has already gathered over 4,000 signatures. 

Goodman Group, the company behind the proposed data centre, recently had to withdraw plans to build a data centre in Lane Cove following community opposition. Gregory Goodman, CEO of Goodman Group, has added a $20 million penthouse in Double Bay to his suite of multi-million-dollar mansions in upmarket Woollahra. He’s certainly not building a data centre next to any of his luxury properties.

Since the initial council information session, community pressure has forced the council to adopt a more moderate stance. It says that it will explore legal avenues to challenge the development. At federal level, sensing widespread hostility to mega data centres, the Albanese government has announced plans to ban them in residential areas in city suburbs. But these regulations will not apply to existing approvals. 

And we cannot leave things in the hands of the politicians and bureaucrats because the law is stacked in favour of big business. We must continue to pressure the state government and local Labor member. 

A community forum on 26 October organised by independent councillor Ahmed Ouf to oppose the project drew 200 people at Guildford Leagues Club. A similar number showed up to the council meeting on 28 October to register their opposition to the proposal.

NSW Socialists have played a central role in this campaign. We have doorknocked thousands of homes in the area, gathering signatures for the petition, talking to local residents.

The NSW government and Julia Finn could intervene to stop this project if they wanted. But they’re more interested in appeasing tech billionaires. That’s just one more reason we plan to take this fight to the next state election and vote Finn out.

Alma Torlakovic

 is the NSW Socialists candidate for Western Sydney’s Granville in the upcoming 2027 state election.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Mass protests defeat the far right in Brazil, but Lula is no way forward
content:
With the winds in Latin America blowing decisively towards the far right over recent years, voters went to the polls in the continent’s most important country, Brazil, in October. The Workers’ Party (PT), led by long-time leader and incumbent president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, lost in the first round, but achieved a remarkable turnaround in the second round.

Lula, as he is popularly known, was running against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, Lula’s predecessor. Jair is currently serving a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup after he lost the 2022 election. During his term he oversaw the deaths of over 700,000 people during the pandemic and is a close ally of President Trump. 

In the first round, Flavio Bolsonaro won 47 percent against Lula’s 45 percent. The right also took control of Congress.

The PT’s first-round loss shows how much support the PT has lost among its traditional base. The outgoing Lula administration was committed to a fiscal framework of zero budget deficits, resulting in caps on public spending and wages. It also allowed further oil exploration of the Amazon. During the campaign, Lula gave ground to the right's tough-on-crime platform, indicating his support for lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16.

The PT’s poor performance in the first round makes its turnaround in the second round even more impressive. Over the three weeks, the PT’s vote increased by over ten million, giving the party 52 percent of the vote. Facing criminal allegations of money laundering, Bolsonaro fled to Miami.

The key factor in the sharp jump in the PT vote was the huge rallies that spread across the country between the two rounds of voting. The day after the first round, students at the Federal University in Rio de Janeiro held an assembly that turned into a rally, spilling out onto the streets. Social media and WhatsApp groups exploded with calls for demonstrations. On 7 October, the National Union of Students called demonstrations in several major cities that saw tens of thousands come out. 

These initial demonstrations were about mobilising to defeat the far right, defending public education, and fighting to reduce the work week to five days from six, a demand that Lula’s government has resisted. Although backing for the PT’s re-election was present, it received much less emphasis. One slogan was: “No to the father, no to the son.”

By 9 October, even small cities were holding assemblies and demonstrations. In Ponta Grossa, a city of around 350,000, university and high school students held an assembly of over a thousand people, promoted as “students against fascism”. It decided on an action plan that included leafleting and door knocking. Similar scenes played out at universities across the country.

“The first few days after the election were like a frenzy”, said Veronica O’Kelly, a national leader of the socialist group Revolucão Socialista. She continued,

“WhatsApp groups promoted rallies across the country. Students led demonstrations out of the universities into the streets. Their demands were immediately far beyond anything the PT was offering. This is what kicked off the mass demonstrations that came over the following weeks.” 

On the first weekend after the first round over one million joined marches in Sao Paolo and Rio de Janeiro under the slogan “The class is in the streets”. Lula was a prominent feature of the rallies, standing on top of a bus in Sao Paolo, surrounded by throngs of people. In other cities, hundreds of thousands joined marches. 

But students remained the driving force. On 14 October, the student union at the University of Brasilia held a demonstration of over 50,000 in the capital under the slogan “Bolsonaro never again and end the 6x1 now,” referring to the six-day work week.

The fact that the rallies raised major economic demands alongside support for the PT put pressure on Lula not just to offer promises after the second round but to take immediate action. On 14 October, Congress passed a constitutional amendment reducing the work week from six days to five with no loss of salary. This was a monumental victory for the Brazilian working class that the movement imposed on not just the PT but the entire ruling class. The measure passed the Senate 75 to 1, with even Bolsonaro’s party voting for it.

Another notable point of the election was several strong results for the left. Several far-left organisations inside the Party for Socialism and Liberation (PSOL), the main party to the left of the PT, formed the Radical Left Caucus, which included several prominent figures like Thiago Avila, a leader of the Sumud Flotilla for Gaza, and other current PSOL MPs. Their platform included a series of pro-working class economic reforms such as the nationalisation of public utilities. Six members of the Caucus, running as PSOL candidates, were elected or re-elected. The combined vote for Radical Left Caucus candidates exceeded two million, showing political space exists to the left of the PT if candidates embrace a more left-wing platform.

Brazil’s election shows that the far-right’s seemingly unstoppable rise to power can be halted. What stopped it was not the capitulatory reformism of leaders like Lula. It was the power of ordinary people, mobilising and organising in the streets, universities and workplaces.

author: Nick Everett
title: Will Israel’s election outcome make life better for Palestinians? Not likely.
content:
In the lead-up to Israel’s 27 October election, media headlines declared this would be the most “consequential” in Israel’s history. At stake is the fate of Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who faces corruption charges at home and an international arrest warrant for war crimes in Gaza.

Israeli politicians debated the cost of living, the independence of the judiciary, conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military, a state inquiry into security failings on 7 October and Israel’s growing isolation abroad. Not up for debate was Israel’s Gaza genocide, nor the massive expansion of Israeli settlements, settler violence and military invasions in the West Bank, nor Israel’s seizure of territory in southern Lebanon and Syria. 

This was a contest between two blocs, a pro-Netanyahu coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties against an alliance of centrist and right-wing Zionist parties seeking to depose him, led by retired General Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff. A third bloc, made up of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, was initially barred from participation by Israel’s Central Elections Committee before the supreme court overturned the ban.

Right-wing parties Likud and Otzma Yehudit petitioned for their exclusion, accusing the Arab-majority parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism. A ban was, however, upheld against Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party and one of the Joint List candidates, on the grounds that he had supported armed struggle against Israel. 

The evidence? An opinion piece published in 

Alaraby

 on 8 October 2023, in which Abu Shehadeh described the previous day’s Hamas-led attack on Israel as a “significant historical event”. 

Accusations of “inciting racism” against Ra’am and the Arab List are of course rank hypocrisy coming from Netanyahu and his coalition partners who have 

called for

 the “total annihilation” of Gaza’s cities and the burning of Lebanon, as well as the death penalty for Palestinians accused of “terrorism” offences.

On the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s social media posts drew attention to long queues of Palestinian voters at polling stations and urged Likud supporters to come out and vote.

“If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi”, he said, referring to the leaders of the two Arab-majority parties.

Netanyahu’s coalition ally and Jewish supremacist Itamar Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout—people exercising their democratic right to vote—as “crazy”. As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has armed Israeli settlers and established a paramilitary police force in the West Bank.

Basel Smotrich, another Jewish supremacist Netanyahu ally, and leader of the Religious Zionism party, announced he had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what he described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters, alleging voter fraud. 

While Netanyahu failed to win this election, he remains far from defeated. His ruling coalition, dominated by Likud, will likely secure 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, a major drop from the 64 seats he won in 2022, and significantly short of a majority. However, the opposition bloc is trailing with 48 seats. The opposition’s only pathway to power is to govern with the support of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, which together secured an additional 19 seats (nearly double the ten they secured in 2022).

This would not be unprecedented. In 1993, the Oslo Accords were signed by a minority Israeli government with the support of the Arab List parties.

In 2021, Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas broke with the Arab List to join an eight-party coalition, the first time an Arab-majority party had joined an Israeli government. For Abbas, this was an opportunity to secure some short-lived investment in Palestinian communities inside Israel, while turning his back on the elephant in the room: the Israeli occupation. The coalition collapsed within a year following defections from its right flank.

Abbas has declared his intention again to seek a coalition that can unseat Netanyahu. His Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on its slate. However, such overtures have so far been rebuffed. 

Israeli musician Yali Sobol delivered Israel’s opposition politicians this blunt message via Facebook 

according to

 the 

Guardian

: “If you stop being racist two amazing things will happen to you. First, you will stop being racist. Second, you will discover you have won.”

However, this is a message unlikely to be heeded by an opposition that is as firmly committed to the Zionist project as Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has said he would consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service, knowing that the Arab List and even Ra’am would be highly unlikely to countenance such a capitulation.

Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance, and Avigdor Liberman, head of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, have throughout the election campaign ruled out such a coalition. 

This opposition bloc has much more in common with Netanyahu and his far-right allies than it does with the Arab-majority parties. Eisenkot, who served in Netanyahu’s government for eight months during the Gaza genocide, is responsible for a long list of 

war crimes and crimes against humanity

, opposes Palestinian statehood, and is credited with being the mastermind of the Israeli’s army’s 

Dahiya Doctrine

, which calls for disproportionate force against civilians.

Bennett served in the Sayeret Matkal and Maglan special forces units of the Israel Defense Forces, before launching himself as an IT entrepreneur and subsequently entering politics as Netanyahu’s chief of staff. 

Accused of

 involvement in the massacre of more than one hundred Lebanese civilians in Qana in 1996, Bennett has openly called for the extrajudicial killing of Palestinians. He 

reportedly told

 a national security advisor, “If you catch terrorists, you simply have to kill them”.

Lieberman, a former Netanyahu minister, is also no stranger to controversy. He has advocated that Israel’s citizens should sign a loyalty oath or lose their right to vote. In April 2018, during the great March of Return, Lieberman justified the killing of at least 189 unarmed Palestinian protesters by 

declaring

 that there are “no innocents in Gaza”, a belief now widely shared by the Israeli public, according to a Hebrew University 

poll

.

General Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, is considered the most “left-wing” of the opposition coalition, and has been the sole leader of a Zionist party to countenance governing with the support of Arab parties. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes”, said Golan, according to a 

Guardian

 

report

. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”

Yet Golan, who was previously the army’s deputy chief of staff, has been one of the most strident advocates of genocidal crimes against Palestinians in Gaza. In an October 2023 interview with 

Ynet

, Golan 

said

: “First of all, close all the electricity switches to Gaza. I think that in this battle, it is forbidden to allow a humanitarian effort. We need to say to them: listen, until the [captives] are released, from our side, you can die from starvation. It’s totally legitimate”.

Where will all this lead? We can anticipate weeks of horse-trading between Israeli politicians to stitch together a coalition. In the liberal media, this is presented as democracy in action. “Israel has always been two things: a Jewish state and a liberal democracy”, the 

New York Times

 

insists

. Voter turnout—the highest in almost three decades—supposedly demonstrates Israeli citizens’ enthusiasm for the democratic process. And “Arab Israelis” (Palestinians) voted in record numbers, making two Arab parties “potential kingmakers”, according to the 

Times

.

Neither claim bears any resemblance to the truth. Israel is and always has been a racist, settler-colonial state. Just like its colonial predecessors, Israel has long pursued a “divide and rule” policy towards its colonised subjects. In 2025, there were nearly 7.5 million Palestinians living in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, according to the Palestinian Bureau of Statistics. Together these 7.5 million Palestinians narrowly outnumber Israel’s Jewish citizens.

Yet, the vast majority—the 5.6 million who live in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem—are denied citizenship and the right to vote in Israeli elections. Crushed under the heel of Israel’s military jackboot, they have no say over who governs them. 

The last Palestinian Legislative Council election was held 20 years ago: and Israel refused to recognise the outcome. Mahmoud Abbas, Palestine’s president, hasn’t been elected since 2005, and has postponed every election since. The Palestinian Authority, though recognised as a “state” by most countries, including Australia, is a toothless and corrupt entity with a history of collaboration with Israel’s repressive security apparatus.

In Gaza, where Palestinians have been the target of a three-year genocidal onslaught, at least 75,000 have been killed. The survivors are now forced to live in tents in just 40 percent of the Gaza Strip, while being starved by a so-called “liberal democracy”.

In the West Bank, Palestinians are not only denied freedom of movement by walls, checkpoints and curfews, but are increasingly the target of settler pogroms, resulting in their eviction from their ancestral homes and lands. More than 11 million Palestinians rot in Israeli jails, either on “security grounds” or for the crime of being in Israel “illegally”.

In this Kafkaesque scenario, the settlers who carry out these violent pogroms 

do

 get to exercise a vote in Israeli elections, and they mostly vote for Netanyahu’s Likud party or his far-right allies.

For all the talk of democracy and multi-party elections, the most likely outcome, and the outcome we can expect to be favoured by Washington, will be a “national unity” government, or rather a grand Zionist coalition from which Palestinian voices are once again excluded. We can expect more of the same for Palestinians.

Nick Everett is the chairperson of Friends of Palestine Western Australia.

author: Ella Marchionda
title: Big opposition to WA government’s mega-university merger proposal
content:
The Western Australian Labor government is pushing ahead with its proposal to merge three of WA’s four public universities despite huge opposition among students, staff and the broader community. If the proposal to merge the University of Western Australia (UWA), Curtin University and Murdoch University goes ahead, the result will be a “mega-university” of 120,000 students, making it the biggest in the country. Both staff and students know that the merger will result in job losses, course reductions, larger class sizes and a decline in education quality. 

The proposed merger represents a corporate reorganisation of our universities to more effectively align with the priorities of capitalism in the state, particularly in defence and resources. Mark Barnaba, deputy chair of mining giant Fortescue Metals, will head the steering committee. 

The state government’s reasoning is straightforward: Western Australian universities are falling short in meeting industry needs, and their research income trails behind that of east coast universities. Nonetheless, the universities are already largely controlled by the needs of industry. Curtin University is already involved in the government’s “Critical Minerals Trailblazer programme,” which aims to “accelerate the commercialisation of university research” by increasing business investment in research and development related to defence and critical minerals. UWA hosts the Defence & Security Institute, which promotes the $368 billion AUKUS nuclear submarine program. 

The main problem with education is not that it isn't sufficiently competitive, but that it’s run as a business. Universities operate as degree factories, treating education as a commodity and students as consumers. University governance boards are more and more led by industry executives and those with corporate and business expertise, placing financial goals at the forefront. 

The corporate nature of universities has been highlighted by huge cost-cutting measures at multiple universities around the country, where staff, students and courses are attacked while executives’ million-dollar pay packages are protected.  Sydney’s UTS recently paid $7 million to KPMG to design course cuts and organisational restructures. Universities use faux crisis narratives to rationalize these cuts, with a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry reporting that six universities exaggerated financial issues to push through course and staff reductions.  In 2021, UWA implemented significant reductions in staff positions and the anthropology and sociology majors.  Murdoch University recently announced that budget cuts were necessary because of a decline in international student enrolments. A university system that relies on international students as cash cows is toxic.  

The proposed merger will only intensify corporate control of the university system. The new university will continue to have overpaid executives and rising student fees. The government-commissioned Deloitte report titled “Rapid Cost-Benefit Analysis” suggests that raising international student fees could increase revenue for the new university. But the recently merged Adelaide University has already revealed serious risks to university staff and the overall standard of education. Last month, the university introduced a voluntary early retirement scheme and indicated that voluntary redundancies might be considered. 

The proposed merger is extremely unpopular: two-thirds of National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) members polled on the plan are against it. On 21 October, 300 students and staff rallied outside state parliament to oppose the merger. The turnout was impressive at the semester's end when students are swamped with assignments.  Students expressed concerns about the potential loss of Indigenous Studies courses, while staff worry the change will result in larger classes and heavier workloads. 

Rojin Didari, a member of Socialist Alternative and one of the speakers, stated what must be made clear: 

“There is nothing good about this merger. It is not about the betterment of our education. It is not about staff and students.  It is about corporate interests.”

Liberal Party Shadow Education Minister Liam Staltari addressed the protest after being invited by Curtin Guild President Dylan Storer. The Liberals are opposing the merger, but they are no friends of students or staff.  Under Scott Morrison, the Liberals brought in the Jobs Ready Graduate Scheme, which has more than doubled the cost of an Arts degree.  John Howard's time in office saw the destruction of universal student unionism. And today, the Liberals want to cut international student numbers.  Staltari was booed off the stage after just 20 seconds because students at the protest knew better than our Guild leaders who our real friends are.

Given the strong pushback, local media report that the merger proposal is losing momentum.  However, we must keep up a big campaign involving students, staff, and the community to defeat the proposal.  Beyond that, we must fight for a different vision of education—one focused on supporting students and the wider community, rather than corporations. 

A recent report 

conducted by the NTEU revealed that the federal government spends two and a half times more money on funding private high schools than on public tertiary education.  The money is there. We could abolish fees and improve conditions for students and staff alike.  It’s a political choice, one that governments of all persuasions are unwilling to make. 

The next protest against the merger is a community rally organised by the NTEU on Saturday 7 November at 12pm, Supreme Court Gardens in Perth.

author: Lance Selfa
title: What to expect in the US midterm elections
content:
The Republican Party, also known as the GOP or Grand Old Party, controls both chambers of the US Congress, allowing President Donald Trump to pursue his far-right agenda with little legislative resistance. But that may soon change.

In the United States, federal elections occur every two years. The congressional midterms, so named because they occur in the middle of a president’s term, will be held on Tuesday. Polling suggests Republicans will be trounced. Voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, who serve fixed two-year terms, and about one-third of the 100 Senators, who serve six-year terms. A range of state-level races, including for governors in California, Michigan and Florida, will also take place.

The Democratic Party is expected to win back control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But just how much difference will that make? 

Lance Selfa

, author of 

The Democrats: A Critical History

 and editor of 

US Politics in an Age of Uncertainty

, previews the elections and what might come after them.

Multiple indicators point to a Democratic victory in the midterm elections. Trump is an historically unpopular president. Gasoline and diesel prices are at their highest in years because of Trump’s war in Iran. 

Consumer confidence is at a 73-year low

, and 

74 percent of Americans

 tell pollsters that the country is moving in the wrong direction.

So it’s no surprise that Democrats are favoured to win the House. In fact, Republicans have given up trying to forestall that. 

Data-driven forecasters like G. Elliott Morris

 and Nate Silver place the probability of a Democratic House higher than 90 percent, and the probability of the Democrats winning the Senate at 70 percent or higher.

The well-regarded 

New York Times

 poll

, published 21 October, estimated that, were the election held then, Democrats would receive 52 percent of the vote, compared to 41 percent for the Republicans. If that holds, it will be the biggest Democrat popular-vote margin in a midterm election since the Watergate scandal brought down the Republicans in 1974.
