That result wouldn’t represent an endorsement for the Democratic Party, which remains as unpopular as the Republicans. But US midterm elections are classically “throw the bums out” elections. And the Republicans, who control all parts of the national government, are the bums this year.

Trump and his toadies declare the polls “fake” and promise a Republican victory. But their behaviour—Trump, Vice President Vance and other administration figures are campaigning almost exclusively in “red” conservative areas—suggests they know they are in deep trouble. Polls currently show that the Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats haven’t won since 1932, is a toss-up. And Democrat James Talarico is slightly favoured to win a Senate seat in Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide since the 1990s.

The last-minute campaign blitz and the truly obscene amount of money billionaires are spending to shore up Republican candidates may limit GOP losses. It seems clear, however, that the Democrats are headed for victory next week. The real question will be how high the Democratic wave will crest.

What will Trump do?

All the above assumes that 3 November will unfold as a “normal” midterm election. But Trump and his minions are talking openly about challenging or overturning the results. Given Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, nothing is “off the table”.

Trump, his captive Supreme Court, and Republicans at all levels of government have conducted a years-long campaign to disenfranchise sections of the population and undermine democracy. This includes the Supreme Court’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act, gerrymandering to lock in GOP majorities, and Trump’s so-far failed attempt to use the US Postal Service to make mail-in voting more difficult.

Trump and his Justice Department have continued to act on the lie that non-US citizens are voting illegally. The DOJ has tried to force state governments, constitutionally responsible for running US elections, to hand over their voter rolls. With voting data in hand, the Trump government says it can purge non-citizens from the rolls. So far, no state has complied, and the courts have ruled against Trump and the DOJ.

However, the DOJ has persisted. In late October, it indicted 28 individuals in California whom it claims voted illegally. Moreover, it sent lists of supposed non-citizen voters to each California county, threatening each with legal action if they didn’t set those voters’ ballots aside. The Trump DOJ has even filed a pre-emptive suit against Alaska—before a single vote is tallied—because it allowed two Republican candidates with the same name to appear on the ballot.

Trump has also increased the harassment of Democratic politicians, such as Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar and Virginia state Senator Louise Lucas, accusing them of crimes.

These tactics are meant to intimidate opponents of Trump, while threatening legal sanctions against thousands of election officials and government workers who are charged with making US elections free and fair. It’s also worth watching what sort of chicanery—from closing polling stations to dropping thousands from the voting rolls— Republican-controlled states will deploy to limit the vote.

There are other more far-fetched tactics Trump and his minions contemplate. They might declare that foreign governments are intervening in the election—which would require the federal government to seize state voting machines. They might deploy ICE thugs, police or the military to polling places to harass and intimidate minority voters who disproportionately vote for Democrats. MAGA hardliners are even calling on Trump to implement “martial law”.

Even though these moves are far-fetched, the 6 January 2021 storming of the Capitol should tell us that they are not beyond a desperate Trump or his lackeys like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Still, to work, they depend on a disciplined and willing chain of command that doesn’t appear to exist currently. Remember, this is the same crew whose failure to make the most basic war preparations allowed Iran to knock out most US military bases in the Middle East.

Whether all of this will work to preserve Trump’s and the Republicans’ hold on the state is unknown, especially if the Democratic victory is as overwhelming as many expect. The Democratic Party is mobilising hundreds of lawyers and thousands of poll watchers to counter them. But if some of these dirty tricks succeed while Trump and the GOP are overwhelmingly unpopular, socialists should be prepared for street mobilisations. Democrats may want to fight it out in the courts, but the balance of social forces will matter more. And this is where Trump’s historic unpopularity has a material impact on events.

Follow the money

The 2026 midterm election is on track to be the most expensive of all time, with billions being spent on both sides. Open Secrets, a non-partisan monitor of campaign spending, noted that “outside groups”, i.e., groups not officially connected to candidates, had 

spent more than $2 billion by early October

. These spending levels would have been considered excessive for a presidential race only about a decade ago.

But as campaign spending—mostly 24/7 television and online advertising—spirals upward, the leverage a small number of billionaires gain over the political system increases as well. By some estimates, Elon Musk alone could spend as much as half a billion dollars to support Republicans. This is more than Trump’s campaign committee spent in 2024. But for Musk and his ilk, this is pocket change.

And even accepting that these are truly obscene amounts of money that amount to legalised bribery of politicians who set the legal framework for capitalist profit-making, they are a small price to pay for the capitalist class and its richest members. We are amid an unprecedented investment boom (

estimated at $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032

) to remake the US economy under the aegis of artificial intelligence “hyperscalers”. A few billion to shape the legislative and regulatory environment is a trivial expense in comparison.

While the liberal anti-Trump opposition has focused on the spending of right-wing billionaires like Musk or the Uihleins of Illinois, we can’t ignore that the candidates raking in the most money in this midterm cycle are almost exclusively Democrats! As 

Open Secrets’ analysis of early October reports to the Federal Election Commission pointed out

:

“Democrats dominate the top fundraising rankings in both [the House and Senate]. They hold the top nine spots among Senate candidates and nine of the top 11 among House candidates.”

The leading Senate candidates, Texas challenger Talarico and incumbent Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff, hold huge advantages over their Republican opponents. And the leading House fundraiser, with the most cash on hand, is 

none other than “democratic socialist” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

! Many Democrats may say that they (mostly) reject corporate political action committee (PAC) money and depend on “individual contributions” from ordinary people. But it’s clear from Federal Election Commission data that most individual donors to Democrats are well-off people associated with the tech, higher education and health sectors.

And if you look at 

Representative Hakeem Jeffries,

 who is set to become Speaker of the House and third in line to the presidency, you will find that he doesn’t turn down corporate PAC money. About 85 percent of his funding comes from business interests. Moreover, corporations launder their contributions through “super PACs”, providing another source of support for candidates.

Democrats may be spineless and feckless, ineffective in delivering for their liberal base when they gain official state power. But the main reason goes beyond character and is better explained by 

Upton Sinclair’s admittedly gendered quip

: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it!”

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), the organisation charged with recruiting and funding Democratic congressional candidates, draws more than 60 percent of its war chest from corporate PACs and rich individuals who can afford $50,000 contributions, 

writes socialist Kim Moody

. Given that, is it any surprise why the vast majority of congressional Democrats are pro-corporate “centrists”?

Two of the most active sectors in political donations—cryptocurrency and AI/tech—have leaned toward Trump and the GOP since Trump retook the White House. But they remain “bipartisan” in their 

approach to winning support in the legislature

 and among state-level politicians. In fact, one leading AI Super PAC runs two divisions: one that 

donates to Republicans and one that donates to Democrats.

The northern Virginia suburbs of Washington, DC, are becoming as reliable a Democratic Party stronghold as New York or the San Francisco Bay Area. But the area also has the largest concentration of AI data centres in the US, 

and the region’s Democratic congressmembers receive

 hundreds of thousands in AI industry donations.

Despite huge bipartisan popular opposition to Big Tech and data centre exploitation of land, tax breaks, power and water around the country, don’t be surprised if a Democratic Congress and the Republican White House figure out a way to pass “reforms” on AI and crypto that will leave ordinary people wondering why they voted for “change” in 2026.

Will it stop the slide to authoritarianism?

In the event of a Democratic sweep, people who despise Trump and MAGA will alternate between celebrating and feeling relieved. But, just as in 2020, they shouldn’t assume that the threat of US authoritarianism is vanquished. This will be so for both specific, “conjunctural”, reasons, and for more general aspects related to our political era.

The first conjunctural reason is the most obvious. Trump will still have the White House and the administrative machinery of the federal government at his disposal even if the Democrats take the Congress. Trump is likely to increase his lawless and authoritarian behaviour while daring the Democrats and the courts to stop him. Even moderate legislation to limit Trump’s tariffs or to restore cuts to federal health care programs will face Trump vetoes.

The second conjunctural reason to keep up the fight is that Democrats may be the GOP’s only alternative on most ballots, 

but they are not an opposition party

. The Democratic Party is a corporate-backed entity dedicated to supporting American capitalism and US empire.

Democrats are campaigning on vague promises to bring “affordability” to ordinary Americans and “accountability” to the criminals in the Trump administration. If they do take one or both houses of Congress, they will become locked in a cage match with an administration that will not recognise Democrats’ authority.

On the “accountability” front, Democrats are already lowering expectations. Jeffries and even leading progressives are saying they want to avoid a 

“performative” impeachment

 of Trump. So, despite condemning the president’s corruption and lawlessness, they are already signalling they don’t want to use congressional power to hold him accountable. On affordability, they are promising legislation 

to reverse some Trump policies

 (back to the Biden 

status quo

), but they are also pursuing the fool’s errand of winning Republican support for them—in a Congress where Republican minorities will be hard-core MAGA zealots. This is a recipe for failure.

The third conjunctural reason is that a Democratic majority in Congress won’t change the fact that a small handful of billionaires exercise more power over policy and ordinary people’s lives than any “democracy” should tolerate. As author Hamilton Nolan told 

New Republic

 journalist Perry Bacon:

“[W]hen money buys influence, and you have these obscene, enormous, nation-level fortunes in private hands, it just at a certain point crowds out the ability of everybody else to influence politics in a way that you have any kind of balance of power.”

The American oligarchy may be in Trump’s circle now, but it can easily move its money and power to influence Democrats as well. Especially when they have willing Democrats like Jeffries or California Governor Gavin Newsom to attend to them. Newsom, a presidential hopeful for 2028, is opposing a referendum for a one-time tax on billionaire wealth to fund state health care programs. That’s how the “affordability agenda” crashes on the shoals of American oligarchy—or is watered down so much that no one even notices it.

The question of oligarchy leads into the general character of the “era” of politics that Trump has come to define in the US. A generation of neoliberal hollowing out of good jobs and government services in the service of oligarchy has 

left the share of wealth going to labour at its lowest level since the 1940s

.

This reality has undermined the legitimacy of the “centre-left” and “centre-right” parties that had dominated the politics of liberal democracies since the Second World War. The far right has surged into political spaces the old parties vacated, while labour and social movements have been weakened.

Lula's come-from-behind victory in Brazil’s presidential election and the landslide defeat of MAGA-friendly Vŭkic in Serbia show that far-right victory isn’t inevitable. But if fighting authoritarianism relies only on electoralism and leaves it to mainstream political parties, we are only one election away from the authoritarian consolidation Trump has so far been unable to accomplish.

So those who will welcome the GOP’s defeat next week shouldn’t look to manoeuvring in Washington. They should draw inspiration from 

mass movements

—like those in India, France, the Spanish state and Serbia, to name a few—for a strategy to put the right on the defensive.

author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

lycéens

title: China’s forgotten miracle makers
content:
History has no parallel for modern China’s economic transformation. To what do we owe the China “miracle”, in which annual GDP growth averaged 9 percent over 40 years, wages up roughly tenfold in 30 years, and more high-speed rail built in ten years than the rest of the world in all time?

In the heyday of globalisation, people said China proved the magic of free markets and free trade. These days, people are more likely to attribute the country’s success to some special Chinese characteristic, such as its state-directed investment or its “Communist” dictatorship. 

These perspectives share in common a wilful or ignorant blindness to capitalism’s real wealth creators. Economic value comes neither from the market’s “invisible hand” nor the state’s “guiding hand”, but plain old everyday hands. The secret to China’s “miracle” is the not-so-miraculous condition of its working class.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Review: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser
content:
Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History

 by US writer and Pulitzer Prize winner Benjamin Moser is a useful contribution to uncover the history of opposition to Zionism within modern Judaism. It traces the history of anti-Zionism from the late 19th Century through the lives of several anti-Zionist Jews across the Middle East, Latin America, Africa, Europe and the US.

Moser begins in the late 19th Century in the Russian Empire, where the deep oppression that the Jewish population faced led to a cultural Zionism that, among other things, sought to revive Hebrew. One of its leaders was Aaron Samuel Tamares. But around the same time, there was also a territorial, national, and racial Zionism being developed by figures like Theodor Herzl. Published in 1896, Herzl’s 

Der Judenstaat

 (The State of the Jews) gave a racial definition to Jewish people, as opposed to the then-dominant idea of Jews being a religious community. It also argued that European anti-semitism could never be eradicated and an independent Jewish state was therefore necessary.

In response to Herzl, the cultural Zionism of Tamares and many other rabbis quickly became an explicit anti-Zionism. title: NT government closes Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter
content:
Residents of Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter were evicted by the Northern Territory government on 12 October, and relocated to Batchelor, a town 100 kilometres away.

Yilli Short Stay Accommodation (YiSSA), which is run by Yilli Rreung Housing Aboriginal Corporation, was home to hundreds of people, mostly Aboriginal. Many have experienced domestic violence and are living with serious health conditions, including kidney conditions requiring dialysis. 

Residents from communities across the territory would stay at YiSSA while accessing medical care or other services in Darwin. Nearly 400 people were directly affected by the closure of the facility, including 160 children.

YiSSA’s closure will place more pressure on remaining homelessness services in Darwin. Meanwhile, the minority of residents transferred to the smaller facility in Batchelor will not have the same access to support networks, food, healthcare and education. Batchelor is a town with a population of around 500, a small health clinic and no public transport.

author: Danica Rachel
title: Operation Paperclip: The Nazis behind the US space program
content:
The Apollo moon landings are some of the most impressive technical feats ever achieved, and, for capitalism’s boosters, definitive evidence of the superiority of Western capitalism over all other social systems. The United States beating the Soviet Union to the finish line in the space race is held up as the ultimate triumph of capitalism over communism. But the path that took humans to the heavens began in the depths of hell: the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp in Nazi Germany.

Built near the town of Nordhausen in central Germany, Mittelbau-Dora provided its prisoners as slaves to the Mittelwerk. This was a factory built under a mountain for the mass production of the V2 rocket, the world’s first long-range guided ballistic missile. The several thousand civilians killed in London and Antwerp by V2s were not the only victims of these Nazi weapons: at least 20,000 prisoners died as a result of the conditions in Mittelbau-Dora and the Mittelwerk.

Edwin Katzenellenbogen, who was convicted for crimes committed as a doctor at the Buchenwald camp, described Dora as “the Hell of all the concentration camps”. Tens of thousands of prisoners worked in interchanging 12-hour shifts, first to dig the kilometres-long tunnels of the Mittelwerk, then on the dark production lines within.

title: Europe’s youth and workers in revolt
content:
The metaphor of a tinderbox is one of the most overused in politics. But how else could you describe the situation in Europe today, where every small spark of resistance seems to be catching and turning into a powerful blaze? 

Things kicked off in France in late September, when students in the working-class suburb of Créteil in the South-east of Paris blockaded their school in protest against poor conditions. This has since grown into the deepest challenge French President Emmanuel Macron has faced in his ten years in power. On October 17, students were joined by workers in a national mobilisation of 800,000. Strikes, demonstrations, blockades and riots have all played a role in this movement. It’s not just the radical left comparing this situation to the legendary student and worker uprising of May 1968.

In Spain, anger at the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose rent was raised 230 percent when her apartment was acquired by an investment firm, has generated a massive movement for housing justice. The streets have forced the centre-left Sanchez government to call early elections, and typically hesitant union leaders to schedule a general strike for November 11.

author: Dougal McNeill
title: Striking for Palestine in Aotearoa
content:
Thousands of workers at universities and polytechnics (TAFEs) across Aotearoa (New Zealand) went on strike Wednesday 21 October, rallying against poor pay offers and the increasing precarity of employment in tertiary education. This was exciting enough on its own terms. The last time we went on strike, in 2022, it was the first in decades, and felt like something new. Now tertiary workers join teachers, public servants, health workers and others who have taken action over the last two years.

Our right-wing coalition government has attacked many of our rights but, in the fightback against their assault on everything from Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the country’s founding treaty with Indigenous groups) to pay equity, we’ve seen that the long drought around industrial action in these islands has been broken by welcome and nourishing rain.

Each bargaining campaign has different priorities and, at Te Herenga Waka in Wellington, my university, one part of our campaign stands out. We went on strike for Palestine. University Workers for Palestine, a campaign group bringing together staff across the country, emerged from the anti-genocide protests since 2023 to make concrete demands of institutions here. author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest. They turned it into a hub for broadcasting news, appeals, morale-boosting content and, importantly, political arguments about the way forward for their revolution. author: Tom Bramble
title: US imperialism in the 21st century
content:
At the start of this century, US imperialism was at its peak. It had been a decade since its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had crumbled; the country was now the unchallenged global superpower. Washington was bringing countries into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that had been the USSR’s satellites in Europe, and it could rely on its allies to extend US influence into every corner of the world.

The US dominated the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and was the most powerful nation in the United Nations. Its economy was booming, and the federal government ran surpluses. US multinationals found new markets and investment outlets worldwide. It was the heyday of “globalisation”. The US ruling class boasted that the country was a beacon to the world. As Democratic candidate Al Gore put it in one of the presidential debates in 2000:

“It is a great tribute to our founders that 224 years later this nation is now looked to by the peoples on every other continent and the peoples from every part of this Earth as a kind of model for what their future could be … The power of example is America’s greatest power in the world.”

Twenty-five years later, US rulers are not so assured. The country has suffered a series of crises, and the global balance of power has shifted. The US remains the world’s leading power, but it is wracked by dysfunction on a series of fronts.

author: Ben Hillier
title: ‘Post-truth’ politics is business as usual
content:

Oxford Dictionaries, which crowned “post-truth” the word of the year when Trump first took up residence at the White House, noted that “it describes not just particular assertions, but a general characteristic of our age”. The 

Economist

“His brazenness is not punished, but taken as evidence of his willingness to stand up to elite power … [Post-truth politics] picks out the heart of what is new: that truth is not falsified, or contested, but of secondary importance. Feelings, not facts, are what matter in this sort of campaigning.”

Yet if “post-truth” is characterised by emotional appeals and relegating facts to the sidelines, it’s not clear that politics has fundamentally changed at all.

On a 2008 autumn night in Grant Park, Chicago, Democratic president-elect Barack Obama, promoted as an articulate Harvard Law graduate with a firm grasp on reality, addressed an enormous crowd. The backdrop was an emerging economic depression: millions of workers were being sacked, more than 3 million homes had been foreclosed in the previous 24 months, the financial system had collapsed, and tent cities of the newly homeless were springing up on the edges of cities across America.

title: Repressive one day, strike-breaking the next: Queensland workers under attack
content:
As if the right to strike hasn’t been curtailed enough. On 14 October, the Queensland Liberal National Party government accepted a raft of recommendations from a review into the state’s industrial relations laws. Restricting the right to strike is central to the changes the LNP plan to implement, including giving the industrial relations minister sweeping new powers to stop workers from taking protected industrial action. 

Under the proposed amendments, protected industrial action can be terminated by the minister “if it would ... cause significant damage to the state’s economy”. The same goes for action that would “significantly disrupt the delivery of a public service”—a direct attack on the ability of schoolteachers, paramedics, hospital workers and others to take protected action. According to industrial law firm Maurice Blackburn, the laws will also restrict the window in which protected industrial action can be taken and give employers the right to dock workers’ pay even in cases where they are still performing some duties while on strike.

The proposed amendments also target any action taken in the lead up to, or during, events such as the Brisbane Olympic games, where the minister simply needs to be satisfied that such action has “a significant effect that is contrary to the public interest” to have the power to terminate protected action.

author: Luca Tavan
title: How the Socialist Party is different from the other parties
content:
Members of the Socialist Party are often asked what makes us different from other parties. Prospective left-wing voters bruised by the long history of politicians selling out their principles want to know how we will avoid becoming part of the same establishment we want to challenge. On the other hand, some left-wing Greens question whether the Socialist Party is even necessary, seeing as their party already offers similar policies. 

The only way to answer these questions properly is to explain how the Socialist Party is unlike any other in Australian politics. We have a vision of society and a political strategy that differs fundamentally from all pro-capitalist parties, from the Liberals to the Greens. So what’s so distinctive about our project? 

Socialism!

The first thing is in the name. We are a socialist party, avowedly opposed to the whole capitalist system. Of course, the meaning of the term “socialism” is contested. Many progressive politicians, from UK Greens’ Zack Polanski to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, have ridden a wave of hostility toward right-wing billionaires and use the term “socialism” to describe their goal of reformed capitalism.

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments where they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

author: Priya T.
title: Eugene Debs—the socialist who won a million votes
content:
Eugene Debs was the most popular and beloved socialist leader in United States history. Famed for exceptional speechmaking, the Socialist Party of America raised $20,000 to buy a train for Debs’ inaugural run for president in 1906. The “Red Special” carried Debs across the country to hundreds of meetings, from the union halls of mining towns to a mass gathering of more than 10,000 workers at New York’s Madison Square Garden. 

A lifetime of struggle, and the lessons born from bitter defeats, transformed Debs from a trade unionist and Democrat to a socialist committed to building a working-class party. 

Debs was born in 1855 in the small town of Terre Haute in Indiana. At fourteen, he started working on the railroads. Railways were central to the industrial expansion going on in the United States at the time, connecting major cities and transporting commodities between them. Capitalists employed gangster violence against unions, keeping working conditions dangerous and wages pitiful. Ray Ginger, in his famous 1949 biography of Debs, writes that in his fifth year on the railways, a friend and workmate of Debs fell under a train and died. Worried he’d meet the same all-too-common fate, Debs returned to Terre Haute shortly afterwards.

author: Connor Knight
title: When Australian socialists dared to dream
content:
In the years after World War One, the Australian socialist movement reached its peak influence. Socialists led big strikes, gave speeches to crowds of tens of thousands and oversaw a flourishing radical press. Thousands of workers believed socialism was possible. But until now, few historians have given this generation of Australian socialists the acknowledgement they deserve. 

Duncan Hart has been a prominent socialist in Brisbane for nearly two decades. 

His new book

, 

From Revolutionary Hopes to Shattered Dreams: The Socialist Movement in Australia:1918-1925,

 brings this momentous period of Australian socialism to life—its revolutionary promise, the fierce debates that animated it and its eventual decline. He spoke to 

Red Flag

’s Connor Knight in Brisbane about the book. 

What inspired you to write this book?

I was inspired by reading about the people in the movement—they were genuine socialists who wanted to overthrow capitalism, not supporters of dictatorships or advocates of gradual reform.

content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.
